This monk had carried a load of dregs from Xuefeng’s place; upon reaching Yantou’s place, he added another load.

It is truly burdensome and, frankly, there is simply nothing that can be done. It has ultimately brought two great elders to exhaustion as they spent their breath attempting to explain it, yet in the end, they did not know where it truly lay.

Thus, while it is true that Xuefeng and Yantou called to one another like elder and younger brothers to stir up and propagate this Way, how shall we understand the matter of "bowing his head and returning to the hermitage" in relation to the "final word"? One must believe in Xuefeng.

Yantou was like a Wheel-Turning Sage King: he issued a single proclamation and gave a single command, and throughout the four quarters and the eight directions, there were none who did not submit and obey.
Why, then, does this monk miss the mark at every turn? If you all wish to have thorough clarity, [you must look further].
You must investigate the Three Turnings of the Tiger Hill [Zhaozhou].

If you penetrate these three turnings, then bowing your head and returning to your hut, the "Final Word" will naturally manifest in every thought-moment. You will attain great freedom in responding to circumstances as they arise;
coming and going within birth and death will leave no trace whatsoever. Nevertheless, although it is thus, when Jiangshan speaks in this manner, he is pointing toward Tiger Hill.
Before his elder brother, he let out a laugh that was not quite full. Why? One should not plant thorns at the gate;
later generations will find their robes snagged by them.
Fellow practitioners, I have been invited to Jingsi. Since I first resided at Zhongshan, drought and flood have followed one after another. Now...

This year it was especially severe. Descending from the mountain with my alms bowl, I relied upon the offerings of the faithful donors who requested me to ascend this seat to proclaim the fundamental principle (*zongzhi*), so that they might obtain its residual benefit as a means for their single meal. Now tell me: what is this fundamental principle?
How is it to be proclaimed? Speaking according to reality, even if all things throughout the great earth—whether grasses or trees—each possessed a broad and long tongue...

As for the mark of the tongue, I am likewise unable to utter a single word. However, because the sincerity of the faithful assembly is so firm and earnest, I cannot help but resort to the secondary gate of meaning to speak here and there, responding to the needs of this moment.

What is called the "essential teaching" (zongzhi) is that which was left unsaid by Śākyamuni throughout his more than three hundred and sixty assemblies—whether speaking horizontally or vertically—yet which now strikes home in a single blow.
My son, at the very end, amidst an assembly of one million people, he held up a flower to show the multitude. Only Mahākāśyapa alone broke into a smile.
Śākyamuni, the Old Man, then bestowed upon him a name, calling it the "Treasury of the True Dharma Eye" and the "Subtle Mind of Nirvāṇa," and entrusted it to Mahākāśyapa.
From that time on, through the four groups of seven patriarchs in India and [the transmission] in the land of Tang...
Two or three. The elder monks of the world have transmitted this directly down to the present day.
If one traces its ultimate source, it does not go beyond the assembly gathered here before us now. Each and every person possesses this true single thought.

Before this thought was clarified, for all those people, in the midst of responding to conditions in their daily lives, they never lacked even a single thread of it by so much as a hair’s breadth. Once it was clarified, for all of you...

In the midst of daily activities and in response to conditions, not even a single hair’s breadth has ever been added. From the highest sages down to those in the six realms of existence, all sentient beings possess this true single thought.
Within the sphere of responding to conditions throughout the days and months, delusion constitutes karmic conditions, while awakening is Buddha-nature.
Thus, karmic conditions and Buddha-nature are separated by no more than a hair's breadth; it is merely a matter of forgetting grasping.

Through the mind of relinquishment, one attains spontaneous liberation wherever one may be. Therefore, the Buddha said that the people of Jambudvīpa have such fierce and intense thoughts that they are most capable of performing both good and evil.
To transcend the four fruits of the śrāvaka path and surpass the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattva, sitting in equality with all Buddhas—this too is brought about by this single thought-moment.
Conversely, to pass through the three miserable realms and the six paths of rebirth, ultimately falling into the Avīci Hell, is likewise due to this single thought-moment.
Even hell is created by this single thought-moment. If those who follow the Way can suddenly realize it in a single thought-moment, then neither good nor evil will be able to confine them.
This is why the Great Master Huineng said to Upāsaka Ming: "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—at that very moment—what is the original face of Upāsaka Ming? Thus it is.
Thus, when the various donors and faithful see this assembly before them in their daily activities and responses to conditions, this single thought-moment is neither bound by good nor bound by evil.
Yet they do not realize that this single thought-moment is like the great sun-disk rising in the east: its pure radiance illuminates everything, leaving no hidden corner unlit.
It is just as when the various donors and faithful give rise to thoughts and move their minds each morning [to encounter this assembly].

Be mindful. Whether in movement or action, in turning, walking, bowing, or looking up, and whether among parents and spouses or between brothers and friends—whether these moments flow toward good or toward evil—not a single one can deceive your own mind.
Since nothing can deceive your own mind, simply, in the midst of daily life and in response to conditions, look with urgent, piercing eyes at this single thought of goodness.

From where does a single thought of evil arise? If you suddenly see through it and know the source from which this one thought comes, then the worldly categories of good and evil will no longer ensnare you;
the twenty-five realms of existence within the three worlds will instantly melt away like ice, and the eighty-four thousand afflictions will be liberated wherever they occur.
When you realize that the whole is your own true, original mind, only then will you have faith.
The Way—from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity and the venerable elders of the world, down to the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the sun, moon, and stars;
and the grasses, shrubs, humans, and animals—whether sentient or insentient—all flow forth from my own single thought, the heart of ultimate reality.
Therefore it is said: "This very mind, mind, mind is the Buddha; the most wondrous thing in the worlds of the ten directions. Its subtle functions are pervasive and sovereign.

Pity living beings. Nothing is as true as the mind. Although the ancients, out of compassion, spoke of "falling into the weeds," they only wished for individuals to clarify this one thought of reality.
Have you not seen that, long ago in the assembly on Vulture Peak, there was a chief disciple who was a mendicant;
he encountered the bhikṣu Aṅgada and asked him: "From where does a mendicant come?"
The mendicant said, "I come from the realm of reality. Hengqie asked, "What is called 'reality'? The mendicant said, "It is named 'reality' because it is quiescent extinction (*śānti*).
"Yet, as it appears before us, the three realms are continuous and the four modes of birth are vast.
Monks are monks and laypeople are laypeople; those who stand stand and those who sit sit. Within, there are seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, along with arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing."
Confusion. Outwardly, the myriad phenomena are arrayed like a forest; one is moved by form and emptiness, light and darkness. Is this quiescence? Or is it not quiescence?
If, at this very point, one does not truly perceive with a single thought before one’s eyes, then one cannot avoid being turned by external objects.
Haengga asked again: "Within the mark of quiescence, is there something sought, or is there nothing sought? The Beggar said: "There is nothing."
Qiu asked, "Hengga, since there is nothing to be sought, why do you seek? Hengga replied, "Within that which has nothing to be sought, I therefore seek it.
Observe these two men: the questioner probes to the very source and bottom to see the depth;
the respondent is like a mirror facing a stand, unable to escape the beauty or ugliness [of the truth]. Hengga asked again, "Within that which has nothing to be sought, why do you seek?"
The Bhikṣu said: "All who seek are empty; those who obtain are also empty; those who cling are also empty;
that which is real is also empty; those who come are also empty; those who speak are also empty; those who ask are also empty.
Even nirvāṇa, the state of tranquil extinction, and all realms of space are likewise entirely empty. For the sake of such a sequence of dharmas of emptiness, I seek the Truth."
O Great Assembly, if that which is attained is not empty, one is burdened by the mind;
if that which is attached to is not empty, one is obstructed and stuck everywhere, failing to achieve liberation; if that which comes is not empty, one is shifted by the signs of movement;
if that which speaks or asks is not empty, one dies beneath the words and is enslaved by speech. [All this applies to] tranquil extinction and nirvana. Everything...
If the realm of empty space were not empty, one would be ensnared by a supreme and wondrous state from which there would be no time of escape;

how, then, could a single moment of true reality ever be revealed? It is just like this mountain monk: this year, all our estates have been submerged by floods and not a single grain has been harvested;
it may be called "empty. Yet when I go down the mountain to hold my alms bowl, wherever I go, I am pressed and constrained by others, unable [to remain].
Enough! Talking east and west, yet never having bestowed so much as a hair’s breadth of real Dharma upon anyone—it may be called empty.
To proceed in this very manner: with this single thought, I speak without speaking; before this assembly, with this single thought, you hear without hearing.
Since there is neither speaking nor hearing, after all, what can be called "the reality"? *Shout!*
With one shout, he said: "What is this 'sleeping talk'?
Master Cong requested [this teaching] on behalf of his mother. As the ancients said: "Sustenance is insufficient to repay one's parents;
only the sage repays them with virtue (*de*). "Virtue is insufficient to reach one's parents; only the sage reaches them through the Way (*dao*). This is the Way.
This is not what the people of the world call the Way; it is the subtle and divine spirit that transcends birth and death—the ultimate Way of the sages.
As for virtue, this is not what the world calls virtue; it is the perfection of all goodness that encompasses both the hidden and the manifest—the ultimate virtue of the sages.
How can it be called the subtle and divine spirit? How can it be called the Way that transcends birth and death? How can it be called the perfection [of all goodness]?

The myriad virtues encompass the merit of both the hidden and the manifest. You, sons of Chan, place yourselves within the monastic groves; purify yourselves and empty your minds to investigate and clarify your own true nature.
If you clarify your own nature, there is not a single thing that is not the True Vehicle, and not a single dharma that is not a wondrous function.
Whether it be the twenty-five realms of existence within the three worlds, the eighty-four thousand afflictions, or the four classes of sages and the six paths of ordinary beings—[all are thus].
Together with all insentient things, they all turn toward this very point, where ice melts and tiles crumble.

At such a time, not only do you repay the parents of this present life with virtue and reach them through the Way, but even the parents of all kalpas past—there are none whom you do not repay with virtue and reach through the Way. Have you not seen how, in the past, the Venerable Upagupta...
At the age of fifty, he had never spoken with his mouth nor ever stepped with his feet. Now tell me:
what was the meaning of his not having spoken or stepped for fifty years? One day, he saw Buddhatrāta arrive at his home.
He immediately rose and paid homage, then spoke in verse: "Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin?
The Buddhas are not my path; who is the supreme path? Nandi replied with a verse: "What you say is intimacy with the mind;
parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice accords with the Path; the minds of all Buddhas are precisely this. This is what constitutes reaching true intimacy."

The Way. To repay one’s parents with virtue is the fundamental root. Consider us ordinary people: we have received our physical bodies from our parents, and it is only after three years that we are finally released from their embrace.
How can you say there is a principle that "one's parents are not one's kin"?
We shave off our hair and beards, don the robes of the Buddha, eat the food of the Buddha, dwell in reliance upon the Buddha, and ought to practice the conduct of the Buddha. How is this so?
I shall explain the principle that "the Buddhas are not my way. You must know that for fifty years, the Venerable Puṇyamitra did one thing alone:

he did not dare speak with his mouth, nor did he dare step forward with his feet. One day, when he encountered the Venerable Nandī, who brandished the precious sword of the Vajra King, he was struck directly upon the throat without even touching its edge, such that Puṇyamitra was completely subdued.
Venerable Dha, that which has obstructed my breast for fifty years has now dissolved like ice melting away. Thus, regarding Nandika’s Way: "Your words accord with the Mind;
they cannot be compared even to one's parents. Your practice accords with the Way; the Mind of all Buddhas is precisely this.
In this way, when words accord with the Mind, they are entirely the primordial parents; when the Way and practice accord, they are the Buddhas.
This mind is not obtained from without. Thus we know that the wondrous spiritual intelligence is the path for transcending birth and death;

it is replete with all virtues and encompasses the merit of both the hidden and the manifest. For fifty years, Vimalakīrti held this clearly within his breast. Though he did not speak, his words filled the world;
though his feet did not tread the ground, he walked alone upon the Great Path. Suddenly, he was encountered by the Venerable Nandī.

It was lit and ignited, until its radiance became magnificent and vast, illuminating the entire universe. It serves as a model for both laypeople and monastics on how to repay the profound kindness of one's parents.
For this reason, today our donors, Zhang Zhang Shengyuan and Wu Zhang Shengyuan, [have made this offering].
Accompanied by the steward Sō, I entered the mountains to observe the one-hundred-day memorial for my late mother, Lady Dai Shōichi.
At that time, I prepared a feast at the Gandha-kuti for the practitioners of the Prajñā path present before me, and thereupon charged this mountain recluse with the task.
Ascending this seat, I shall proclaim the vehicle of the school. Whatever excellence I may bring forth shall serve to support their posthumous blessings and repay the kindness of my parents.
This is truly what is meant by "excellently reaching one's parents" through the Way of our Sage, and "excellently repaying one's parents" through the virtue of our Sage.
Generally speaking, for all those born between heaven and earth—whether monastic or lay, whether at home or...

There is filial piety for those in the household, and there is filial piety for those who have left the household. For those in the household, it consists of serving one's parents with propriety while they live, burying them with propriety when they die, and making offerings to them with propriety.
For those who have left the household, it consists of investigating the wondrous and enlightened mind and traversing the path beyond birth and death.

Having been refined by all manner of goodness, you are clothed in virtue that encompasses both the hidden and the manifest. Should you be able to attain internal clarity and illumination, then this Way and this virtue will appear vividly before you.
Reaching such a state, above there is no debt of unrequited gratitude, and below there is a path that may be practiced.

Upon hearing this, you will recall that your honored mother, the Lady, was by nature gentle and modest, never tiring in her delight for the good; for she was endowed with such gentleness and humility.

This nature naturally accords with the good within daily life. Whether dwelling in leisure, eating, resting, moving, or turning about, there is not a single action that does not accord with ritual propriety.
Thus, throughout the mornings and evenings of each day, one has no leisure for other tasks, but makes the study of the scriptures and the recitation of the Buddha’s name one’s primary duty.
At the very moment when one has no leisure for other tasks, it is precisely when the virtuous mind is pure and ultimate. This virtuous mind...
Once one has attained such purity and perfection, then the sutras one reads are the sutras of one’s own mind, and the Buddha one contemplates is the Buddha of one’s own mind;
all of these flow forth from within the nature of one’s own innate warmth and humility.

As for receiving guests at one’s door, exerting every effort in hospitality, and relieving the hardships of others as if they were one’s own urgent concern—were it not for a lifelong devotion to goodness without weariness, who could achieve such things?

It is thus: even at the moment of death, one may request fragrant water for bathing, gather the members of one’s household and kinsmen, and assemble one’s sons and grandsons to stand in a circle around the bedside so that the final instructions may be imparted: "After my passing, I shall surely be reborn in a good realm;
you need not dwell upon my loss. Furthermore, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha until my eyes close, never ceasing from your lips. Generally speaking, at the point of death—

At the threshold of birth and death, there is no room for falsehood. Observe how our late mother, the Great Lady, having spent over ninety years in this human world manifesting in a female body, conducted herself with gentleness and governed the multitude with humility. She took joy in doing good without weariness.
Now that the time has arrived, she has fulfilled her final instructions; truly it can be said: "O Son of the Buddha, if one can skillfully employ [the mind] in all circumstances..."
This refers to the fact that such a mind attains all supreme and wondrous merits. Long ago, there was an old woman to the east of the city who had been born at the same time as the Buddha;

she did not wish to see him. As soon as she saw the Buddha approaching, she covered her face with both hands, yet the Buddha suddenly appeared between his ten fingers—there was truly no place to avoid him.
I ask the assembly: tell me, did the old woman to the east of the city not [see the Buddha]?
I pray that you may see the Buddha. As for your late mother, the Great Lady of the Hall, she never ceased reciting the Buddha’s name from her lips at the moment of death;

was there any difference in the quality of their practice? Before this assembly, if one can only penetrate the wondrous spiritual intelligence and attain the path of transcending birth and death, refining oneself through myriad virtues and being graced by the merit of both the hidden and the manifest, reaching through to the very top and bottom with complete clarity, then one will know how to repay [one's parents].

Lady Ta-jun and the old mother from east of the city—these two are the places of descent. If one can know the places of descent of these two, then one knows the place of descent for each person’s own self.
If one knows the place of descent for each person’s own self, this is the wondrous spiritual intelligence.
This is the path for transcending birth and death. It is replete with all manner of goodness and envelops the virtues of both the hidden and the manifest.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day, there is no moment when it does not manifest before one. Once this manifestation is attained, one suddenly and equally transcends both the mundane and the supramundane;
humans and non-humans are indistinguishable in their nature and characteristics. Only the whisk of Mount Jiangshan does not enter into this protection.
Society. Why is this? The Three Sages certainly have not yet clarified this principle; how could the Ten Sages reach this school?

In China, the ocean of the teachings is profound and deep; ten thousand treatises and a thousand sutras are all subsumed within it. The Chan gate is vast and expansive, encompassing all six classes of ordinary beings and four types of sages.
Each member of the monastic community bears a spirit as lofty as the heavens, overturning the ocean of the teachings.

Throughout the thousands of sutras and myriad treatises, there is nowhere for it to leave its trace; the Gate of Chan is shattered, leaving no place for the four classes of sages or the six realms of ordinary beings to find shelter.

Thus, both Chan and the Teachings are merely provisional names. For forty-nine years, the Yellow-Faced Old Man preached at length and in depth—discussing emptiness and existence, essence and characteristics, sudden and gradual, partial and perfect—yet he could not avoid using the five colors in vain to paint the void.
Emptiness. The blue-eyed barbarian monk came ten thousand *li* from the West, pointing directly at the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha.
Without cause, he needlessly bestowed a bowl and forcibly attached a handle to it. Xuanzhi, who among us does not possess these goods?
If you can simply turn within yourself to seek them, you will naturally attain liberation wherever you are. Have you not seen that in the past, Chan Master Heshan Shoupu’s left...
Mian Ren was by nature bold and unrestrained, refusing to be controlled or constrained. His character was lofty and his insight sharp and quick.

He lectured on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*, engaging in debate with the assembly on difficult points and questions. His arguments were manifold and versatile, moving freely in every direction;

none dared to confront his intellectual acumen. He frequently criticized Guifeng Zongmi’s commentaries for containing much speculative interpretation, pointing out their errors as a warning to students.
He said, "This is not to be trusted. There were some elder masters and veteran scholars among them who all reproached him, saying, "Guifeng was certified by the National Teacher Qingliang.
How dare you cast aspersions upon him? This is what is called 'an anthill trying to shake a great tree. Fupian sighed and said:
Those who study today have long been deluded by fame and status. Qingliang and Guifeng did not possess three heads or six arms;

why, then, would they have willingly subjected themselves to such humiliation? It was because their integrity was lofty and their insight was clear. Although they were scholars of the written word, they were no longer deluded by the written word.
Had they engaged in formal inquiry and consultation, there would have been great illumination, even had they followed the traditions of the past.
If there is anything the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not yet reached, they must certainly rectify it. At that time, the Venerable Huangbo Sheng returned from Jiangxi to Baofu in Chengdu.
Lü Longtu, whose name was Dafang, was the military governor of Chengdu; he treated him with the etiquette of a disciple and visited him daily for instruction.
Although Fuyu was by nature bold and unrestrained, refusing to be bound by formal constraints, he nevertheless harbored doubts regarding this matter. Thereupon, he changed...

Fu served as a secret listener to their discussions, yet he did not understand a single word all day long. Consequently, his mind was filled with indignation and his mouth was parched with frustration.
Returning home, he lay down and gazed at the ridgepole of his house, saying: "In the past, Master Sheng was renowned for his scholarly exegesis, and Master Lü was the foremost sage of the age;
they exchanged views with such mutual respect and faith. Yet I do not believe them. While my doubts remain unresolved, I sit here [in this state]."
It is due to a lack of learning. Generally speaking, when investigating this matter, one must possess a certain kind of spirit before it can be achieved.
He then departed from Sichuan and arrived at Jinnam Jinluan, where he heard that there was an old monk in the assembly who had once met Master Qing’an of Lianshan;
the monastic community regarded him as one who had "thoroughly investigated" the Way. Fuping then questioned him, saying: "In what way do the sutras and treatises contradict Chan?"
The Master [Zongmi] often saw elderly practitioners who frequently disparaged and reviled him. Why was this? An old monk said to him:

"Those who study the treatises on karma and the scriptures do so because they take them to be matters of emotional consciousness and intellectual principles—the boundaries of thought and measurement. These cannot by themselves give rise to the holy or bring about the realization of the Way.

Even if there were those who did give rise to the holy or achieve the Way, they would have used the scriptures and treatises merely as conditions. If one does not rely on self-realization and self-awakening, how can the scriptures alone suffice?"
If these treatises were authoritative, then all those in the world who are able to read, recite, know, and understand them would have simultaneously realized the holy state and attained the Way;
how could they then be willing to labor wearily, bowing and scraping among us within the monastic groves? This is all the more so regarding the sūtras and śāstras.

These are all dead words on paper. In the schools of teaching, they call this the "obstruction of the known" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). How could it possibly give rise to sagehood or lead to the realization of the Way?
As for the common saying among teachers of doctrine that "the known is not the obstruction; rather, the obstruction obstructs what is known," I myself formerly attended their lectures.

I have listened to various lecturers as they expounded upon the meaning of the "Chapter on the Obstructions of Knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). They turned the text over and over again, offering elaborate digressions and prolix explanations that were ultimately unintelligible.
Therefore, based on my own perspective as a mountain monk, I shall briefly offer a critical assessment directly within the context of our own daily lives.

It is just as I, this old monk, said earlier: those who study the treatises on karma and the scriptures take the conceptualizations of their own consciousness, their intellectual principles, and the boundaries of their thoughts to be the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, while you are investigating, pursuing, and contemplating these conceptualizations and intellectual principles, which among them is the mind that knows?
If you [cling] to these conceptualizations and intellectual principles during the time of contemplation—
When the object is perceived before one, if one sees through to the very mind that knows and realizes it is fundamentally empty, then the object known is naturally stilled.
Thus, one perceives that outside the object known there is no knowing mind, and outside the knowing mind there is no object known.
Since both mind and object are empty, their nature and characteristics are equal. Even if you achieve this much, in the gate of the patch-robed monk, it is like the heavens.
The grounds are vastly different. For this reason, the Great Master Daruma came from the West specifically to declare: "A separate transmission outside the teachings.
This old monk wishes to investigate the point where everyone has universally missed the mark; thus, he proceeds by means of the conceptual frameworks of the sutras and treatises.
He questioned him: "As it is said in the sutras, 'All sentient beings are originally Buddhas. Do you believe this?
Puhui replied, "How would I dare not believe the words of the World-Honored One? The old monk said, "If you already believe, why have you come all this way in such great effort?"
Puyu said, "I have heard that the Chan school possesses the principle of a 'separate transmission. That is why I have come. The old monk replied, "This is not something you can believe;
it is not within the realm of belief. Generally speaking, the essential point of the direct pointing of the Chan school has no other explanation;
it is simply the fundamental matter of one's own nature, manifest in the daily activities of every person. For instance, as soon as Śākyamuni was born, he pointed at heaven and earth with his hand."
He said, "Only I am honored alone. This is the clear and manifest revelation of the essential point of direct pointing, intended for the awakening of people.
When he saw the morning star and awakened to the Way, he then said, "How marvelous!

All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata," and "All sentient beings are originally Buddhas," and so forth. From this, one knows that our Buddha [taught] in successive layers.
By means of the essential direct pointing, [the truth] has been opened wide with eight characters and cast into the very laps of everyone.

Yet, we who are his disciples are unable to realize it face-to-face; instead, we search for words and chase after phrases within the thousands of sutras and myriad treatises, willingly sinking ourselves into the realm of language, names, and forms, remaining lost and failing to return. Thus, [it is said: "To reach..."
Master Ma came across the sea and directly took up this matter, explicitly stating that "it does not rely on words and letters," but "points directly at the human mind,
seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha. Therefore, the old monk uses the words from the sutras— that all sentient beings are fundamentally already Buddhas—
to sternly rebuke and interrogate Puhua, as if placing a single iron caltrop upon him.
Although Fupu did not immediately attain realization upon hearing this, there was a persistent sense of obstruction within his chest—a certain thing that remained clogged and refused to dissolve.
At the very moment it failed to dissolve, he reached a stage of gradual realization and insight.
He then asked, "Where does this illness lie? The old monk said, "If you can see Zen Master Huanglong Nan, he will surely enable you [to resolve it]."
His illness was cured. Thereupon, on that very day, Puhui set out. Upon arriving at Huanglong, he asked Chan Master Nan:
"When Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, 'Aside from the transmission of the golden robe by the World-Honored One, what else did he transmit?
Kāśyapa then called out, 'Ānanda! and Ānanda responded. Kāśyapa said, 'Throw down the bannerpole in front of the gate. What was the meaning of this?"
What is the point? Observe how he establishes this point of inquiry; he simply follows along from the lecture hall. His fault stems from following Guifeng’s speculative assertions.
Furthermore, failing to understand the discussion between Huangbo and Lu Longtu, he says, "My doubts remain unresolved," which arises from his own limited learning.

Moreover, he follows the old monk [Yunmen] in treating the sutras and śāstras as mere intellectual constructs and rational principles, falling within the realm of conceptual thought and mental measurement.
From where have you come? Zen Master Nanyuan of Huanglong was a man whose vision surpassed his age; he could see the ailments within another’s heart, liver, and five viscera.
Without deviating by even a hair’s breadth from the point of inquiry, he asked him: "Venerable sir, you came from Sichuan;
did you ever visit Yuquan? He replied, "I did. He asked, "Did you ever stay there? He replied, "I left after one night. Nanyuan said, "A wise man."
"At the site of enlightenment (Dōjō), when General Guan makes offerings, how long has he been forming a karmic connection? What harm is there [in that]?
These words are precisely the commentary on "upsetting the banner-pole in front of the gate. Although Master Pu remained silent for a long while, he again raised his previous question;

this was exactly the moment when Pu’s doubting mind was about to shatter, the contents of his chest were melting away, and he was on the verge of manifesting sainthood and attaining the Way. —Master Nanyue.

He then bowed his head. This may be called "killing a person without using a blade; bringing a person to life without using a sword. Puguang attained great enlightenment on the spot and suddenly forgot all that he had previously realized.
He rushed out in great astonishment and said: "The 'Tigers of Meaning' from the two rivers cannot withstand a single spittle from this old man.
Seeing him at such a moment, having gained entry, there were no words with which to respond and no principles with which to defend oneself; he could only say: [The text ends here.]
Liangchuan Yihu was not worth even a single spit from this old man. Later, when he appeared in the world, he resided at He Shan.
As he was about to pass away, he accepted a memorial offering from the people of a temple; immediately, he sat upright and departed. An ancient said: "Under great doubt..."
There must be great awakening. A small doubt leads to a small awakening; without doubt, there is no awakening.
If one traces the source of this awakening, it cannot be anything other than the doubt regarding the principle of the "special transmission outside the teachings.

This doubt was so profound that, were it not for Master Nanyue, who casually made him bow his head to strike at the disease in his very vitals, how could he have reached the state of great peace and bliss? Only then did he realize that [his former understanding] was inverted.

It is the same principle as the pole at the gate of a temple; the site of practice for the wise, the ritual offerings made by General Guan, and the moments when one bows the head—all follow the same path. When one arrives here, neither Chan nor Teaching can take hold;
neither Buddha nor Patriarch can take hold. In this place where nothing can take hold, everything takes hold. Thus, though one spends the entire day with sutras and treatises, [one remains free].
Not falling into the realm of words and speech, though throughout the day one may be a sage or an ordinary person, one suddenly forgets the traces of rising and sinking.

Entering birth and exiting death, one attains great freedom. Between the mundane world and the world-transcending, there is not a single dharma remaining. To proceed in this manner is still but a minor resting place, a temporary livelihood.
One must further know that there was a time before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had arisen, before Chan and the Teachings were established—when the grain...
Shan had not yet left the lecture hall; it was only when he encountered the one move of Master Nan that he finally attained realization.
You all, if you wish to know where this one move lands, simply follow the example of Chan Master He Shan Pu, who, upon seeing Master Nan, attained a great awakening once and for all;
then it will naturally become clear without needing to ask others. Even if you have not yet discerned the beginning of it, in the future—

To Shian Shou (formerly the abbot of Tianning in Pengzhou):
The old fellow Gautama exhausted his verbal karma, speaking crosswise and lengthwise, yet from the beginning there was not a single word of substance for others to savor.
Even when Master Bodhidharma came specifically from the West to transmit the mind-seal alone, it was not even the size of a needle’s point.

Agreed. To engage in the investigation of principle with others, one must be such a person—one possessing natural magnanimity who, at all times and in all places, investigates and scrutinizes the essence prior to Gautama’s appearance in the world and before Bodhidharma’s coming from the West.
When the time arrives, with a sudden burst forth, one clearly perceives one's original ground and thereby knows that Gautama never appeared in the world and...
Mozhao never came from the West. Everywhere and in every place, the constant light is manifest before one; in every land and within every atom, it has never been an external object.
Even if you can do so, this is still but a minor resting place, a temporary livelihood—it is not yet the matter of the School of the Patriarchs.
Have you not seen how the Great Master Yunmen said: "Even if you speak horizontally or vertically as you please, it is still not the matter of the School of the Patriarchs"?
"What is this 'clanging of a hot bowl'? The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon are but a dream; Bodhidharma’s coming from the West was a dream.

Yunmen reveals it in this way—tell me, does this truly suffice for the affairs of the Zen school? Since I have been the abbot here myself..."
I have also been among men, prattling on from east to west; yet regarding the matters of the Zen school, I have never even dreamed of them.
If someone were to bring down a lethal blow and strike this mountain monk to death, it would not be considered out of place. The Head Seat Yanshou is extremely resolute in his pursuit of the Way;
when he suddenly came to bid me farewell and sought my words, I suddenly said: "I shall deal the blow myself. To which I simply replied to him: "Excellent."
To serve as a path for those who know the Dharma heirs among the monastic community,
the true mandate is fully upheld— like sparks from striking flint, like a flash of lightning, like thunder rolling across dry land, suspended in mid-air.
It is like a rock falling from a cliff; one has already missed it before even blinking an eye. These are the ancient masters of old who have trodden this single path.
Whenever they casually let fall a pivot or reveal a realm, people naturally leave the mud and water behind, and their eyes are opened.
From the beginning, they never possessed any real dharma to give to others. Have you not seen how Master Liang-sui went to visit Magu? Magu said:

As soon as he saw him coming, [Baizhang] went to weed the grass. When Liangsui arrived at the place where he was weeding, Baizhang paid him no mind at all and returned directly to his quarters, closing the door behind him.

Liangsui then knocked on the door. Baizhang asked, "Who is it? Just as Liangsui was about to answer, he suddenly attained enlightenment and said, "Master, do not deceive me! Had I not come to pay my respects to you, I would have almost been lost."
"Sūtras and śāstras have caused one to waste an entire lifetime. Now tell me: did Magu have an instruction or not? If you say he had, what did Magu point out?

He said to the people: "What you all know, Liang-sui knows entirely; what Liang-sui knows, you all do not know.
Liang-sui has grasped this very core, and thus possesses the eyes to bring the living to life. Yet, when scrutinized, he cannot avoid being like a beggar who suddenly becomes wealthy.
At that time, in the lecture hall, there was suddenly a man who would not be deceived; he turned the situation upside down.

Face-skin. Look at him—Liangsui had no place to set foot. This Dharma heir, serving as the guest prefect, already knew from the lecture halls of the Brocade City that there was a great matter outside the teachings;
he traveled specifically to Nanquan to seek someone for definitive discernment.
He went twice to the mountain hermitage where the Way was gathered, yet the Mountain Monk said, "I am immersed in the sea of human affairs; I have no leisure to go weed the fields. Nor...

One will then realize that the sutras and śāstras contain points that deceive people. If there are points that deceive people, then it is precisely at those points where one knows for oneself, while it is certain that all other people do not know.
If this is so, then one has not yet left the lecture hall, nor has one emerged from the Gupdaṅga (瞿塘) gorge; the journey of a wandering monk (*caryā*) is already complete.
Why wait until traveling back and forth for a mere eight thousand *li* before considering it an attainment? Nevertheless, upon returning to the lecture hall—
Within the hall, you must by all means refrain from leaking any news. Should you suddenly run into someone who turns their face around, do not say you did not warn them.

The Dharma was transmitted through six patriarchs before reaching Caoxi. After Caoxi, Nanyue gathered its residual venom and unleashed its cruelty upon the rivers and lakes.
The "Horse Colt" was poisoned by it, killing eighty-four people, each one of whom was left in a state of frantic agitation.
Only Baizhang, under a single shout, recovered his impoverished life and sat atop Mount Daxiong.
[The Master] struck the top [of his head]. "Fortunately, you poor fellow! You have been pointlessly seen through by Huangbo.
He calls this 'the function of great capacity,' which brings disgrace upon Linji, who possesses only a single eye. From then on, it was passed from one person to another;

This caused Yuanwu to be caught in the sound of Xiaoyu; the poison manifested before him, infecting Ying'an, who was brought to his death beneath the claws and fangs of the sleeping tiger.
Fortunately, there was a broken sand-pot that allowed him to rise again, until his blazing vitality filled the space between heaven and earth.
When one exhausts its point of origin, no trace remains; when one investigates its place of application, [it is likewise unfindable].
There are no traces. All of this is intended to shatter the old molds of various quarters and to awaken the spiritual mechanism of the thousand sages.
Lately, this poison has been seen to sweep away everything until nothing remains, utterly devoid of breath.

Yet, Master Wukai, having risked his very life, has unleashed this remaining poison from within that state of breathlessness to bestow upon those who come to study. Thus, the orthodox lineage of Bodhidharma shall not fall into silence.
Liao! To show you, Senior Seat Zhìyī:
before all Buddhas appeared in the world, there was a truly fine and peaceful realm. Then, when [Śākyamuni] held up the flower at Vulture Peak...
After the Eye of the True Dharma was entrusted to the Golden-Colored Dhūta, the world suddenly saw the clash of arms, and the four seas were shrouded in dust and gloom.
The Seven Patriarchs of the Western Heaven briefly displayed their sharp blades, while the Two or Three Masters of the Tang Land reciprocated with swords and halberds.

This brought misfortune upon the descendants of later generations, each claiming a single region and vying with one another in a frantic clamor. They mistook south for north and turned water into ice; this has never ceased.
There was one person who clearly perceived where the Eye of the True Dharma falls. Only the two great elders Yunmen and Fenyang were slightly superior;

one said "Universal," and the other said "Blind. Although each extended a hand to uphold this Eye of the True Dharma, wishing to make its radiance brilliant and resplendent, they did not realize that they were instead making it appear increasingly dark and murky. Thus it was.
To proceed in this manner is like the zither of a pure ancestral temple: with its vermilion strings and wide sound-holes, one note is struck and three sighs follow;

there is a lingering resonance. Thus, our late master Mian obtained that lingering resonance and called it "the broken sandpot," casting it onto a heap of refuse where no one could understand it. Only the Elder Songyuan knew where it fell, and he let it go.

He brings forth a stubborn donkey and kicks it to pieces with a single blow; he simply wishes to maintain this well for himself before the Buddhas appeared in the world, so that its transmission may endure infinitely in future generations.

To reveal the threshold of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the "nose-ring" of the patch-robed monks (as demonstrated by Attendant Hui, former abbot of Yanfu in Quzhou): this is not something that can be realized through cleverness, sharp wit, broad vision, or extensive learning;
nor is it something that can be attained through lofty faculties, eloquent debate, silence, or the forgetting of words. Even if one were to possess thorough...
The Heavenly One’s strategy is that of a world-transcending hero. He knows before it is raised and understands before it is spoken; yet even this does not capture his true likeness.
You must, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day and night, turn the light back upon yourself to reflect. It may be better not to understand at all than to falsely grasp anything.
If you harbor even a hair’s breadth of false grasping and take it to be right, that itself is birth and death.
Fundamentally, it is simply a matter of taking a step back in a single flavor. Retreating within oneself and investigating in silence, the more one retreats, the more power there is;

the more one does not understand, the more it becomes manifest. Suddenly, at a certain point, if one steps off the track, one will break through everywhere—thousands of places, ten thousands of places.

Only then will one see that former cleverness and sharp intelligence, extensive learning and vast knowledge, lofty wit and eloquent discernment, and even the state of silent oblivion where words are forgotten—all these are [but empty constructs].
This is the samādhi of one’s own self-enjoyment. It enables one to deceive the worthy and mislead the sages;

to break the two into three, and to take up a single blade of grass and turn it into a sky-reaching long sword, wielding the power of killing and giving life with total freedom. With a black bean, one exchanges the eyes of all people in the world.
Neither sages nor ordinary people can fathom it. Having reached such a state, is this not the threshold of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the very core of the patch-robed monks?
For now, let us rejoice that there is no connection [to be found]. Attendant Liaohui, because his devotion to the Way was so earnest, traveled westward to visit his parents.

A Record of the Established Principle Presented by Zhongding (Former Abbot of Xingshan Monastery in Mingzhou):
If one discusses this matter, it cannot be approximated through intellectual eloquence, extensive learning, or powerful memory;

nor can it be attained by remaining silent, forgetting words, clarifying the mind, or practicing meditative concentration. Even if one were to strike sparks from flint and, within that flash of fire, attempt to grasp it...
It is attained. Within the flash of lightning, one is driven forward by the whip; this is precisely the act of a spirit-squanderer.

To devise a livelihood within the realm of intellectual conditions, or to seek subtle understanding within the nature of reality—all such things are but demonic delusions that cling to grass and settle upon wood.

If you do not proceed in this way at all, there is naturally a path for turning back; yet even this is merely wandering outside of the realm of folly and madness. Therefore it is said: "The thread..."
A hair’s breadth of attachment to thoughts regarding the karmic causes of the three miserable realms will, in a mere flash of emotion, result in shackles for ten thousand kalpas.
Know that this matter is such that as soon as it is thus, it is not thus; the phrase of affirmation is erased, and the phrase of negation is also erased.

If there is even the slightest trace remaining or anything left unexhausted, one is entirely a member of the retinue of heavenly demons and externalists. Only those who have attained this can emerge from all perilous difficulties.
Having left behind all habitual patterns and traps, one remains perpetually at ease—like a fool or a pillar—yet is not bound by this very state.

When it is brought forth spontaneously, it naturally tears asunder the past and present, shaking heaven and earth, so that every person throughout the entire world may individually and thoroughly penetrate this matter.
Thus liberated alone and without dependence, one does not follow these many paths.
Zhe also has not yet reached the fundamental root of this matter. Have you not seen how Sanjiao addressed the assembly, saying:
"If one discusses this matter, the mere lifting of a brow is already to have missed it"? At that time, Magu stepped out from the assembly and said: "I do not ask about missing it."
"What is this matter? Sanjiao said, "You have already missed it. Gu then overturned the meditation seat; Sanjiao then struck him.
This is a living path—step upon it and you will know. Although these two great elders walked hand-in-hand, they could not avoid each pursuing their own destiny.
As for this matter, one has not even dreamed of it in a dream. —Recorded by Secretary Zongding.
Having long traversed the monastic forests, you are deeply conversant with this matter. Let me ask you, Secretary: where are those two great elders?
You have not even dreamed of the place that pierces the nostrils of everyone under heaven; there is nothing beyond these few words.
Should you hesitate for even a moment, wait until this mountain monk has replaced your tongue, and I shall leisurely explain it through for you, Secretary.
The Way is shown as it is recorded in the scriptures:
True Suchness is unmoving, yet its dynamic function pervades the three realms. The ultimate principle transcends words, yet words fill the four quarters of the world.
It is just like the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Bodhidharma facing the wall—this is True Suchness in its immobility; this is the ultimate principle where words are forgotten.
If one can discern this clearly, then one will know that the World-Honored One never actually held up the flower, and that Bodhidharma never sat facing the wall.
The ultimate truth of True Suchness is entirely like a flower in the sky; both movement and speech are but dream-like affairs. One's own field is perfectly manifest everywhere;
before a single stroke of the brush-tip has revealed its color, heaven turns and earth revolves—this is the application of a single pivot.
Before a word was spoken or a silence maintained, ghosts wailed and spirits cried out. Thus, without even leaving the Qutang Gorge, the quest for instruction in the south was completed;
without moving a single step, one has already arrived at the mountain of one’s own home. If this is the great matter of traveling as a mendicant, you have not seen it even in a dream.
Have you not seen how Shitou addressed the assembly, saying: "Words and activities have no connection [to the Way]"? Yaoshan said:
"Even to reach a state where there are neither words nor activities still has no connection. Shitou said: "In this place, not even a needle can pierce it.
Yaoshan said: "In this place, one plants flowers upon a stone; this is a path of life. Step upon it and you will know. These two great elders walked hand-in-hand together.
Although each may hasten toward their own destination, they must nonetheless arrive at the same time. As for the great matter of traveling on pilgrimage (*xingjiao*), you have not even dreamed of it.
As the Record Keeper says: "For a long time he has roamed with the Old Man of Tiantong; as for the great matter of traveling on pilgrimage—"
This old man will surely explain it through to its breaking point. My enthusiasm for the rivers and lakes has subsided, and with a vast sense of resolve, I have the intention to return home;

thus, I have come to test the waters. Taking this paper from my sleeve, I seek words as an essential exhortation. However, Mount Jiangshan has always been dry and barren—like planting flowers upon a rock where a needle cannot pierce.
If you wish to know its depth or shallowness, simply realize it before you have even seen Tiantong.
To Zen practitioner Shizong Ren: You are a high-minded gentleman who has traveled through the monasteries of Mount Lu.

Having prepared a single, authentic mind and body, you have left the monastic groves to enter a spiritual community (*boshe*), seeking teachers and choosing companions solely to thoroughly clarify your own nature and fully comprehend birth and death. If you do not act in this way, you are merely a tourist sightseeing the mountains.
Playing with water, one needlessly wears out one's straw sandals until the soles are worn wide; this brings no benefit to oneself.
Therefore, the Great Master of Yongjia said: "I traveled across rivers and seas, traversed mountains and hills, seeking teachers and visiting paths in order to study Chan.
Since I recognized the road to Caoxi, I have known that birth and death are of no concern. When the ancients gave such a report, it was already complete.
Entering the mud, entering the water—if one is such a person, capable of mastering the pivot and penetrating change, then without shifting a single inch, they alone span the Great Square.
They overturn their own mountains and rivers, exhaust the primordial seas and rivers, and beneath their feet, they sever the life-force of Śākyamuni;
from the tip of their staff, they gouge out the eyes of Master Bodhidharma. There is no path.
One may visit [a teacher], yet there is no teacher to consult; one awakens teacherless wisdom and unleashes spontaneous intelligence.
Have you not seen how Master Xiu of Longji consulted Zen Master Dizang Chen a second time, saying, "I still have matters that remain unresolved"?
This time I have traversed many mountains and rivers and have undergone great hardship. Dizang said, "Those many mountains and rivers were not bad for you either. Observe him!
Kṣitigarbha! Without expending the slightest bit of effort, bring it forth. This shall not merely serve as medicine for the dragon to cure the ailment of outward-seeking;
it shall cause the seeking-mind of all people throughout the entire earth to melt away like ice and crumble like tiles.
Zen practitioner Zongren, a dharma-heir of Tietan, wishes to travel to Mount Lu and has requested a verse from his sleeve to assist him on the journey.
The essence of the Way is simply this: regarding the many mountains and rivers shown by Kṣitigarbha, they are not unfavorable to you. Look with urgency;
if you suddenly pierce through to the point of Kṣitigarbha’s application, you will see that at all times and in all places, there is no wasted effort.
With every lift of a foot and every movement of a step, you are entirely upon the road of Caoxi. Thus one knows for certain that life—
"Death does not concern one another. The face of Mount Lu manifests everywhere.

Even if you attain such a state, you must further know that there is a point prior to when the Buddhas appeared in the world and before the Patriarchs came from the West; only then may you be called a high-ranking traveler."
Jiangshan has already shown no regard for his own verbal karma; now that you have personally beheld the true face of Mount Lu, your own nostrils have been knocked out at once.
Only upon returning to the Iron Pagoda Hall and having the Master pat your back and emit light will you finally see that Jiangshan’s failure was no small matter.

To show the lineage transmitted from the patriarchs to the *vina* (chant leader): acting according to the precepts, it is not merely a matter of the grass before the Dharma Hall being ten feet deep, such that heaven and earth and the great land are all at once left desolate;
even that would not approximate the reality, let alone the talk of "three old women and two grandmothers."

Yellow roads and black paths; exhausting the nature and principles of reality, discoursing on the profound and subtle, and discerning between the ancient and the modern. They devote themselves to silence and stillness, letting their spirits roam through contemplation and observation.
They establish extensive schools and open wide the doors and windows, using flutes and drums to stir the men and women of the households, claiming that this is the true lineage of their ancestors.
Truly there is such a thing. It is much like "a Cao gate coming out of Zhengzhou. These venerable seniors of old possessed great vision;
from the very beginning, they were free from hesitation or deliberation. Yet when it came time for them to bring it forth in practice, it was like Zhang Daoling’s vermilion brush.
When casually raised, it naturally causes rocks to split and cliffs to crumble; gods cry out and ghosts wail, and those who watch cannot even blink.
When scholars of the Way reach this point, unless they possess great roots and have immense power, they often retreat in awe at the precipice.
Have you not seen how Master Xinghua one day said to the rector Kebin: "You do not..."
[He] had long been a master who proclaimed the Way. Kebin said, "I do not enter this monastery.
Xinghua said, "Do you enter because you understand, or do you not enter because you do not understand? Kebin said, "It is neither like that. Now tell me:
did Kebin’s response accord with Xinghua’s intent? If it did accord, why did Xinghua strike him immediately?
He was punished with a meal of coarse rice and driven out of the monastery. If one cannot find a true accord, why did he succeed Xinghua?
Under the patriarchs, one is loathed for having nothing beyond these few things. Observe how father and son were like water and milk;
though their meeting was subtle and wondrous, they could not avoid mutually frustrating one another. At that time, had Xinghua simply followed his orders...

This practice is the true lineage of Linji; it has not reached such a state since the time of the Patriarchs. The Venerable Chan Master Weina came personally from the assembly at Huazang Temple to join us here.
As for the staff with which Xinghua struck Kebin, in all the world today, there is only one person who possesses it: the old master Chun’an.
When one contemplates the moment of the battle of wits, it is certain that he possessed extraordinary skill. It is a pity that I lack the means to determine antiquity and modernity.
I have distinguished this through my own eyes. Although you were rowing your boat upstream against the current of principle, you had no leisure to explain it thoroughly to me;

yet, were we to meet again by chance on another day as you head south, you would be defeated without even being examined. Only then will you realize that under the patriarchs, the command was never issued in vain.
The assembly at Green Mountain has not yet dispersed.

To the Abbot Huìjì, he showed that Bodhidharma came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha. But tell me: does such a thing exist, or does it not?
What matter is there? If you say it exists, you bury yourself; if you say it does not exist, you betray the former sages.

This single lineage, though it covers all like heaven, supports all like the earth, blows everywhere like the wind, and shines everywhere like the sun—nevertheless, there is no place for you to understand it, nor any place for you not to understand it.
Even if it were to exist, it would not be established; even if it were non-existent, you would not be attached to it. Do not seek it.
All the sages do not value their own spirits, for they are fundamentally and naturally true from the beginning, requiring no effort or cultivation.

To acquire something through study is precisely to become a spirit that clings to grass or wood, a ghost-child guarding an ancient tomb. How much less could one intend to settle the mind upon it or apply focused effort to investigate it?

To dally in the realm of silent stillness while wandering within the domain of speech, to cling to the difficulty of reconciling natures, to analyze the subtle and dissect the profound, to examine antiquity and debate the present, and to align principles with affairs—this is like steaming sand to make rice; how could it cure the pangs of hunger? It is like digging into the earth to seek the heavens.

Do not look up at the stars of the Milky Way. Travelers on foot—everyone is equally one who has worn out their straw sandals; it is best to take a single, decisive step that overturns them all, causing heaven to collapse and earth to crack.
Moving everywhere without a trace, looking in all four directions with no obstruction, driving the winds from all eight sides, even ghosts and gods cannot fathom you.
What need is there to speak of Bodhidharma coming from the West? Even the Yellow-faced Gautama would have to beg from your hand for such a thing.
Disciple: Although you have for now clarified the matter of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West, you have not yet clarified the matter of Bodhidharma’s not-yet-coming.
Tell me, what is the matter of Bodhidharma’s not-yet-coming? There is a great teacher named Gao Yuan at Ruiyan on Mount Tiantai;
he has reached the very source of the Dharma and is skilled in expounding the essentials of the teaching. Go there, offer incense, and pay your respects.
Question: What is the future matter of Bodhidharma? This old man will surely explain it through and through;
he will then leisurely come to Mount Zhongshan and invite Elder Wood to serve as your witness.

When the Chan practitioner Siyuan was shown the single proclamation of the Dharma-vehicle, the twelve divisions of the teachings crumbled like falling tiles and melted away like ice. When the Patriarch’s command is put into practice, all people throughout the great earth [are transformed].

With their sharp edges lost and their tongues tied, beyond the realm of Vipaśyin, they claim to have attained self-awakening without a teacher; these are truly nothing but those who lean against walls and huddle by the side of buildings.
To understand that one single pulse—how is it any different from a jackal howling even while still in the mother’s womb? One must know this!
Were it not for a person of great capacity who can take up the entire burden, one cannot avoid being submerged head over tail within a bag of antiquities.
Have you not seen how Deshan, before he had even left the gorges, was still naturally pitiable;
yet as soon as he reached the South, at the place where the paper candle was blown out, he was struck by the poison of Longtan. Once this poison erupted, he simply clung to a single...
He brandished his white staff; whenever anyone approached, he struck them from head to toe.
To this very day, the people of the entire world have been unable to endure the pain. Nevertheless, not a single person has yet known the origin of this pain.
Master Siyuan, having ceased his lectures to travel on pilgrimage, is one who possesses the will for the Way. If you know the origin of this pain, you will see the Virtue.

Before the mountain had even emerged from the gorge, his very life was already in Longtan’s hands. Before the paper candle had even been extinguished, Longtan’s heart, liver, and five viscera had already been seen through by Deshan.

Thus, having come ten thousand *li* from the south, his mother-given countenance was clearly manifest in every place; yet when he returned westward to his original dwelling, in every land and every atom, it was suddenly— (Note:
The final phrase "頓" [dùn] implies a sudden realization or a state of being abruptly revealed, often used in Chan contexts to denote the immediate manifestation of one's true nature.)
Manifested. If this were not yet so, you would strike your own toes on the path ahead; only when you suddenly awaken will you realize that Jiangshan was talkative.
This is shown to the practitioner Haiyin.

In general, those who carry their bags and shoulder their bowls, leaving the monasteries and entering the sangha communities, visit venerable masters to investigate and clarify the great matter beneath the *kāṣāya*.
They must attain complete penetration from top to bottom so that their constant radiance manifests before them, becoming free and at ease.
Truly, even the twenty-five realms of the three worlds and the eighty-four thousand afflictions of worldly toil cannot confine them; they remain unconstrained in their ordinary state.
Take a single step, and the entire universe and the great earth tremble.
Speak a single word, and all the sayings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from antiquity down to the present melt away like ice and crumble like tiles.
Even reaching such a state is still called a temporary crossroads or a minor resting place; it is not yet the Great Matter beneath the *kāṣāya*. How much less...
Chasing after words and following along with phrases, they run outward in pursuit. Within the causes and conditions of past and present, they dissect the profound and subtle.

At the corners of meditation platforms in all quarters, they savor the drool of wild foxes, taking this as their lifelong practice. They claim that the matter beneath the *kāṣāya* robe is merely this; truly, it is as the saying goes:
"One may dwell in hell for kalpas, yet there will be no time of escape. Have you not seen what the ancient masters said? "Hell..."
Hell itself is not yet suffering; it is the failure to clarify the matter beneath the *kāṣāya* that is the ultimate suffering.

When the ancients gave such a warning, although they were all equally mixing mud and water, there was a subtle and essential point within it. If one is a lion that can turn its body around, its tracks vanish as it leaps back.
To a great *icchantika*, even a Buddha does not recognize them—what further "matter beneath the *kāṣāya*" could there be? Hell.
He has remained for kalpas. Furthermore, where else could he be placed? He possesses a spirit that transcends the school and differs from the common eye;
so why worry that the true lineage of Bodhidharma will fall into desolation? Master Haiyin has long traversed the monastic forests and now intends to travel westward.
I passed by Mount Zhong; we parted after seeing one another for the first time. Furthermore, as there was something yet to be said, I have penned these words and sent them to you.
If you were to speculate upon this paper, I, this mountain monk, would surely fall into the Avīci Hell.

To Master Zongliang, the Librarian, he showed a kōan that is already established: it does not involve the slightest trace of attachment; it pervades the earth and encompasses the heavens, enshrouding both the present and the past. To attempt to reach it with the calculating mind is to miss the mark.
"Clearly facing one another, yet separated by the Western Heaven. To accept this with total detachment is still to be a man who clings to grass and wood.

You should know that regarding this matter, there is no place for you to find understanding; it must be your own self. You must possess a mind and body forged from solid iron, and be willing to sacrifice your very life.
Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, investigate it closely and practice it constantly. Suddenly, strike a blow of incomprehensible clarity.

Kill! When encountering circumstances and meeting conditions—whether attending a teacher or seeing a friend—if you are lightly touched by it, it will be like waking from a dream or seeing the sun after the clouds have parted.

Only then will you realize this matter: that it pervades the entire dharma-realm as the root-source of the mountains, rivers, and great earth, and serves as the fundamental essence of the four sages and six classes of beings.
It is stored within the person, in the space of one's own heart; it is not manifested from any other place. Always...

It is revealed at the crown of the head. Having reached such a state, it is precisely the right time to seek out a master with a great furnace and a cruel hammer—one who will subject you to a thousand smeltings and ten thousand refinements to strip away all those shadows and glimmers previously revealed at the crown of your head.
Then the eyebrows remain only above the eyes; the nostrils stay as they were, with the head hanging down. One may simply follow conditions with expansiveness and let one's nature roam at ease.

Even if one gives rise to compassion and wields pity, casually grasping a single thread of the Way, it will naturally shake the heavens and stir the earth, severing the root-source of birth and death for all people and shattering the nesting grounds of the holy and the profane. Truly, this is not in vain.

Regarding my lifelong aspiration for the practice of *xiéjué* (wandering as a mendicant), have you not seen how Master Mazu, when asked by Shuilao, "What is the great meaning of the coming from the West?
gave him a single kick to the chest that sent him tumbling down?

When Shuilao rose up, he clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and the immeasurable subtle meanings are all realized within a single hair-tip. Thus, one recognizes the source.
Go! Now tell me: from where does this single hair-tip come? If you can know its place of origin here, you will see that Master Ma’s “passing the ladder to the thief” was not the work of a true adept.

If you say it was all Master Ma taking up a single thread to cut off the root of birth-and-death for others and shatter the nests of sages and ordinary people, you do not recognize Master Ma at all—not to mention the rest.
The Master’s way of employing [the Dharma] has indeed betrayed his original intent for practicing the Way.
In the world today, there is only the Old Man of Changlu who truly understands Master Ma’s way of employing it. Zongliang, the Abbot, should go and inquire of him;
you will see that before your feet have even crossed the threshold, you will first be given a kick—do not say I did not warn you.

I, the monk Wenjie, am a man of will and practice from my native Sichuan who has traveled on pilgrimage. Having traversed ten thousand li and braved the perils of the Three Gorges, I did not set out merely to tour prefectures and counties or to view scenic sights;
rather, it was solely because the mind of birth-and-death remained unclear that I cast myself into the monastic forests.
In the midst of this, seek out a teacher and choose a friend, hoping for even a single word or half-phrase to liberate yourself from birth and death.
However, this matter depends solely upon the individual to cultivate a long-term resolve and establish a firm determination. Day and night, three times each, one must strive diligently;

throughout the twelve periods of the day, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, silently maintain the practice and earnestly investigate it, until one’s own [nature]—the three hundred... [is fully realized].
From the sixty joints of the body and the eighty-four thousand pores, extending to the entirety of heaven and earth, form and emptiness, light and darkness—
there is not a single hair’s breadth that is not my own mind, which is ignorant of birth and death.
If you investigate in this way and maintain this awareness from morning until night without interruption, when the time comes and you encounter circumstances or objects, [the truth will manifest].
Perhaps provoked by a teacher or a friend, one suddenly lets out a "dumb" sound; the past and future limits are severed, and the three great kalpas are emptied.
This very mind that was previously ignorant of birth and death is, in that instant, like ten suns shining together, or like meeting an old friend in a bustling marketplace.
Only then does one realize the originally possessed thing, which has all along been right here. Students of the Way, you must attain this.
When one reaches such a state, out of ten there are five or six who all nod their heads and swallow their saliva here, claiming they have attained ultimate joy.
Little do they realize that this is precisely the very root of birth and death.
Were it not for a master of great insight who employs the methods of a venomous insect to rot their bowels and sever their life-roots, they would inevitably fall back into [the cycle].
Clinging to grass and perching on wood, they remain within the ranks of wandering spirits and solitary ghosts with no way to emerge.
In this day and age, there is but one master who employs such a means, and that is none other than our venerable elder, Tiandong.
Traveling monks often covet life and dread death, refusing to draw near to this old man; yet having heard that Master Jie has already staked his very life, [they may now approach].
As he was on his way, before he had even crossed the Qiantang River, he was struck by a poisonous vapor that severed his life-root and completely transformed his very bones.
Thus, not only did he not fail in his original vow to travel, but it also proved that my words were not false.
To the attendant Shijie and recent students:
These days, those who carry their bags and bear their bowls go to visit spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), seeking companions and choosing associates;

in every place they go, they gather in groups of hundreds and thousands, all claiming, "I am traveling on pilgrimage" (*xingjiao*). Yet when asked, "What is the matter of traveling on pilgrimage? out of ten there is not one who can answer.

There were five pairs who stared with wide eyes and gaping mouths; some said they did not know, others said they did not understand. Some shook out their sleeves and left, while others covered their ears and departed.
Some raised a finger or extended a fist, some raised their eyebrows or blinked their eyes, some drew a circle, and some performed a woman’s bow.

Circling the meditation platform, he stood on tiptoe, manifesting a thousand kinds of demonic wonders and ten thousand varieties of skills; yet all were but a vast expanse of karmic consciousness, lacking any fundamental basis.
As for the great matter of traveling on pilgrimage (*xingjiao*), it is truly not yet accomplished. But what, after all, is the matter of traveling on pilgrimage?
Simply, throughout the twelve periods of the day, reflect back upon the moment you first set out, leaving the forest groves and entering the monastic communities. All...

Now, when the guidance of a wise teacher and the encouragement of virtuous friends and good companions concern this great matter of traveling on foot—whether one reaches it or not, whether one has penetrated it or not—it all resides within the square inch of one's own mind. One does not need to wait for another to point it out or annotate it before finally knowing it to be thus.
As for the news of having already penetrated and reached the very bottom, not even a single thread of hair has ever been added.
The message has not yet been fully penetrated nor reached its ultimate depth; it lacks nothing by even a single hair’s breadth.

It requires only that, in one's daily life, one never forgets it and maintains an uninterrupted continuity of mind. Suddenly, like a person from a village of three families at the place where they till their fields—
Having picked up a single grain of the Golden Elixir, one takes it casually; immediately, the entire household seems to ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
Whether one has attained penetration or not, whether one has reached the ultimate bottom or not—all of this dissolves like ice melting and a fortress crumbling.
One seeks this square inch of ground, yet it is utterly unobtainable. Only then, from that place where nothing can be obtained, does one grasp a single thread of hair and put it to use.

Once it emerges, it will naturally cover heaven and earth, one by one. Thus, you may manifest a thousand kinds of strange apparitions and employ ten thousand varieties of skills in every place, causing all people to know that there is this "Great Matter" of traveling on foot (*paryaṭana*).
Even if you reach such a state, it is still but a vast expanse of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), with no fundamental basis to rely upon. Ultimately, how is it?
A man with clear eyes has no fixed nest or pattern. To set aside external objects is superior; to pursue them is inferior.
Those who penetrate through this are brilliant on all eight sides; those who do not penetrate through cannot avoid dying beneath the words. How can one not exert oneself? Attendant Shijie.

Seeking a method for self-exhortation, I have thus recorded this to show it to you. If you can place your trust beyond the mere words and their meaning, the great matter of traveling on foot will manifest before you;
only then will you not have failed the essential point I have shown.
Shi Zong, the Treasure Keeper, once related how Muzhou encouraged Linji to inquire about the Great Meaning of the Buddha-dharma from Huangbo.

Although Linji asked three times and was struck with severe blows each time, commentators remarked that he had entered the furnace and crucible three times without being tainted by poison; yet they failed to realize that he had already been deeply pierced by Huangbo.
...the poison is exhausted. It is simply that one does not know the source from which this poison comes. As for that Muzhou, one wonders what kind of eyes he possesses.
He further said to Huangbo, "The Upāsaka who has come to inquire is most in accordance with the Dharma. If you take leave of the Abbot, use skillful means to receive him;
in the future, he will penetrate deeply and become a great tree, providing cool shade for all people under heaven. If indeed...
This is a cool, shady great tree; would it ever consent to being pierced and carved by others?
Upon reaching Dayu, this poison erupted, enabling him to land three punches on Dayu and strike down Huangbo’s entire assembly.

Observe how he recognized the source of this poison and employed it the moment it was brought forth—how could it be anything less than making heaven mourn and earth grieve, ghosts wail and deities cry out? Even if the thousand Buddhas were to appear, they could not [quell it].
What can be done? Nevertheless, one has already been subjected to such arrangements by others.

At that time, when Muzhou urged him to inquire about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma from Huangbo, he immediately employed this fist and brandished this palm; had he done so, the lineage of Huangbo would have been far more than it is now.
Later, he came to monopolize a single region and specialized in employing the "single shout" as his primary practice, as swift and imposing as a long sword leaning against the heavens.

The sword is as dull as a holeless iron hammer. As for the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, the four kinds of critical examination, and all manner of ghostly antics performed therein—these are all manifestations of this very poison.
Throughout the vast monasteries of the world today, how many people can truly know the origin of this poison?
