If you wish to know, simply grasp it at the moment before Linji met Huangbo.
The Dharma-treasurer Zongbao has long gathered with me in the Way. He presented a sheet of paper seeking words as a means of self-exhortation;
I have therefore produced this to entrust to him, to show it to Attendant Zu Yin.
The Patriarch Bodhidharma came from the Western Heaven bearing the seal of no-character;
he has stamped the gates of the face of every person throughout the entire world until none remain who have escaped the net. Alas, there are now five pairs who do not know where they have fallen.
In these present times, the veteran elders of the monastic forests each claim for themselves that they can employ this seal.

They are like people from a village of three households who falsely style themselves emperors, only to bring about their own execution. If you wish to be a true descendant of Bodhidharma, you are worlds away from it.
Only one who possesses the magnanimity to swallow Buddhas and sentient beings in a single gulp will truly understand this seal.
At the very moment it falls, one is able to seize it with the hand of faith; at every place, one stamps and breaks through the gateway of the human face—thus, one will not be disgraced.
This is the seal that Master Guling received from Baizhang; having obtained this seal in his hand, he then employed it.
In the presence of his preceptor, he handled things perversely and applied them in reverse, failing to observe established custom.
One day, while bathing his teacher, he scratched the teacher’s back using this seal incorrectly, causing it to emit light and shake the earth in a place where there was no Buddha.
To this day, this remains on people’s lips. When the attendant Zuyin returned because his teacher had grown old, he said, "If your teacher had emulated the deeds of Guling..."
To verify what you have attained, try to bring it forth.
To Attendant Zu-hui (who was serving at Zhi-ping): "The Buddha-dharma has grown thin;
the Way of the Patriarchs is in decline. There is nothing like this today. Yet, occasionally there is one or half of one who possesses the will."
Regarding the Way, their natural aptitude is not high and their spirit is not expansive. They are eager for immediate results and forget the ultimate fruit;

they become complacent and take pleasure in worldly splendor. If a master accords with them, they rejoice; if he opposes them, they become angry. When shown the realms of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they delight in following them;
when forged with the methods of yakṣas and rākṣasas, they are terrified and abandon the path. Desiring Buddhahood...
The flourishing of the Dharma and the prosperity of the ancestral way—is this not difficult? When Linji saw Huangbo’s severe blows, he knew his home upon hearing the words of Dayu.
When Deshan saw Gaoting beckon him from across the river, he immediately strode across.
Huangbo and Deshan acted for others in such a manner—tell me, was this contrary or compliant? Is it the realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or that of the yakṣas?
This is indeed the skillful means of a rākṣasa. Here, one must possess the innate talent of Linji and the majestic bearing of Gaoting;

only then can one clearly distinguish between the ordained and the laity, and carry forth the burden of practice. The flourishing of the Buddha-dharma and the prosperity of the ancestral way depend entirely upon this.
Shiji Nengjingtou once said:
"If a person wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, they should purify their mind so that it is like empty space;
far removed from delusive thoughts and all attachments, let the mind be unimpeded wherever it turns. What is the realm of the Buddha? It is originally one's own.

The Way of daily practice resides within one's own mind; it is intended solely for the person themselves. Yet, day after day, they remain buried in their heads, drifting along with circumstances amidst every event and object.

To attain resonance with the realm of the Buddha, one need only ensure that throughout the twelve periods of the day, there is no interval between thoughts and not a single moment of abandonment from the heart. Suddenly, as if encountering an old friend in a bustling marketplace—*A!* (a sudden realization).
So you have been right here all along. Upon reaching this state, delusive thoughts and all grasping instantly melt away like ice.

Every phenomenon and every object becomes the wondrous functioning of the Self; thus, one may manifest the sixteen-foot golden body upon a heap of refuse, or the insects in a latrine pit can profoundly discourse on the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Whether calculating strategy or drawing water, it is none other than oneself—sweeping the ground.
Washing the vat—none of these are other things; they are like empty space, which contains all phenomena yet makes no distinctions among any objects.

To proceed in this manner is still merely a minor resting place. Unless one encounters a master of great capacity who, for the practitioner's sake, turns everything upside down and opens up a separate, living path, one will inevitably remain sitting here, facing toward [the old ways].
To escape this ocean of poison where one rises and sinks headlong with no hope of liberation, you must first purify your own heads;

you must directly and fiercely awaken, attaining thorough and penetrating clarity, making liberation your ultimate goal. Only then will you meet the masters of all quarters who possess the great skill and hand of a true patriarch.
I shall certainly be able to pierce through this for you.

To show that the Way of the great ancestral masters has fallen into decline, it is because those who act as teachers do not reach far back into the source, but instead focus exclusively on words and language.
They dazzle others with their knowledge and views, using them as tools to ensnare students. Yet these students lack great resolve;
they merely follow what the world admires and what the age practices, willingly sinking themselves into the realm of knowledge, views, and verbal expression.
Yet they do not know how to turn back; teachers and students delude one another like foxes.
When looking back at the meaning of the plucking of the flower and the smile, or the facing of the wall and the settling of the mind, can they not feel shame in their hearts?

In general, without the substance of the plucked flower and the facing of the wall, one is unfit to be a teacher; without the capacity for the smile and the settling of the mind, one is unfit to study. Although...

It is said: Since antiquity has long passed, the transformations of the age have increasingly declined, and the hearts of men have become ever more corrupt. The pure has daily become diluted; the thick has daily become thin.
The spirit of "plucking the flower" and "facing the wall" no longer arises; those who find peace through the "smile" are not always found.

Yet they do not realize that this Way exists throughout the world, remaining exactly as it was even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas*. It is simply one and the same day.

There are those who, in this very moment, attain sudden realization upon the ground. They enclose neither worldly dharmas nor Buddha-dharmas within their grasp; ordinary sentiments and saintly understandings are shattered without remainder.
They do not fall into the realm of verbal expression, for they naturally possess claws and fangs that transcend the school and differ from the common eye.
When these are casually brought forth, they not only thoroughly cleanse the evils to which the world aspires and the habits of the age, but—
To point at a flower or face a wall is already to deceive people; to smile with a settled mind has not yet attained solitary liberation.
If one can truly act in this way, what need is there to worry that the ancestral Way will not flourish?
It is said that when Zhiguang, the attendant, encountered Meng, he learned archery from Houyi; having perfected the Way of Houyi, he then killed him.

For those in the lineage of patch-robed monks who seek teachers, choose companions, inquire after the Way, and practice Zen—even if they were to perfect the Way of Houyi, if they lacked the resolve to kill Houyi, they would still fail to escape being merely...
This is but a spirit clinging to grass and perching on wood, a ghost-child guarding an ancient tomb. What use is there in such a thing?
This mountain monk understands nothing at all; nor do I possess the skill of Houyi to learn from. Even if I harbored the intent to kill Houyi, I would have no means to carry it out.

To show this, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, the golden-colored *dhūta* monk broke into a smile; when Bodhidharma faced the wall, the Second Patriarch sought his mind but found it utterly unobtainable.

From that time forth, the authentic succession was passed down through the four groups of seven in India and the two groups of three in the land of Tang, like water being poured from one vessel into another.
Not even a drop leaks through. This is all because the ridgepole above is crooked and the pillars below are uneven.
It has reached the point where the entire forest of monasteries across the great earth debates at length, all saying: "Does this single-transmission mind-seal exist? Does it not exist?
If you say it exists, where is the spirit and bearing of a true man? If you say it does not exist, consider how the various regions are filled with pagodas and temples.
Looking at one another, each claims to point directly to the human mind. But how can this be resolved? A man of clear eyes has no fixed patterns;
taking things away is superior, while chasing after things is inferior. Try to realize it before the flower was held up and before the wall was faced;
there is the style of Linji receiving the staff from Huangbo. Only then can you truly study. Without Huangbo striking Linji...
How could Linji’s staff ever be taken as a teacher? Today, throughout the vast expanse of the South, masters and disciples deceive one another like fox-spirits;

those who do not take Huangbo and Linji as their standard, I know them to be sinners within the Buddha-dharma, leading others to become seeds for the hells—is this not a matter of great lamentation? Master Zuqing, the Librarian, requests these words.
I show this to you for this reason. If you act according to what has been shown, the Buddha-dharma will not fall into desolation.
This is shown to Attendant Deying (who resides at Chao-hua).

For those in the lineage of patch-robed monks, leaving the monastic groves and entering the jewel society, they desire directly to penetrate birth and death and transcend the Buddhas and patriarchs. Thus, regarding birth...
The transformation of death is what all people fear; how can one transcend it? The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is what all people desire;
how can one transcend it? If there were a man of vast capacity here—one who cannot be turned back by calling and cannot be confined within a cage—[he would transcend both].
Solitary, perilous, and precipitous; wandering alone without companion, one then perceives that since there has never been birth, how could there be death?
What is there to fear? Since there has never been a Buddha, how could there be patriarchs? What is there to seek?

Whether one penetrates or not, whether one transcends or not, regarding the transformations of birth and death and the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, there is not even a single hair’s breadth of obstruction or hindrance. Thus it is said:

Subsequently, though facing birth and death in every thought-moment, one is not terrified by birth and death; throughout all places, though encountering Buddhas and Patriarchs, one is not constrained by Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Only then is one called a "monk who has accomplished the task," truly not failing the lifelong purpose of one's practice.
If it were otherwise, then throughout the twelve periods of the day, one would be deluded by the transformations of birth and death and deceived by the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
To have no share in liberation is to dwell in the kalpas of hell; can one not exert oneself?
He was shown by the South Attendant from Jiangxi, who wished to request words [of instruction], to go and visit the Venerable Fajian of Mount Jing. Upon hearing this, I paused for a moment.
He arrived. He related the words spoken from the high seat [by the Master]: "This summer at Mount Jing, ten thousand fingers have gathered as a community.
The mouth is atop Mount Lingxiao, while the rice is under the jurisdiction of Pingjiang. It is easy to bring the mouth to the rice; it is difficult to bring the rice to the mouth.
That rice is made of grain—everyone knows this well. But tell me, what do you call the 'mouth'? (After a long pause, he said: "The Great Old One, the Great Old One."
Great! He shakes his two pieces of skin, yet his mouth does not even recognize them. Old Man Fojian has opened the gate of great giving;
he does not refuse those who come. Nan intended to go see him and requested the words of the mountain recluse.
This man is entirely mouth and entirely food—how could one ask whether it is easy or difficult to succeed? Even if Fojian had two pieces of skin, there would be no place to apply them.
Now, let me see: for thirty years, this mountain monk has never once set down a wrong footnote for anyone.
To the Head Seat Wushang Fayan, I show the Supreme Dharma Seal.
Since the Yellow-Faced Old Man [the Buddha] gave it away at the place of the flower-picking, after that single mistake of entrustment, it has been passed down through successive generations.

From the four groups of seven patriarchs in the Western Heavens and the two or three masters in the land of Tang, the elder monks throughout the world have transmitted and conferred this seal one upon another down to the present day.
Though they have "taken the wrong for the right," if one investigates the point of error, there is no other method involved; there is nothing else that is confusing or deceptive.

It simply requires great men of measureless capacity today to transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness, to leave behind the paths of sages and ordinary beings, and to uphold this Dharma-seal within a single [moment].
In every instance, they hand the seal to others, breaking open their face-gates so that each person may take what is mistaken for what is correct.
To know this supreme Dharma-seal is to obtain it not from another; thus one does not fail the Yellow-Faced Old Man’s intent in entrusting it once and for all.

Yet today, as monasteries stand side by side and those who occupy positions call themselves teachers, none fail to claim for themselves that they have grasped this Dharma-seal—yet when it comes to studying the Way...

These practitioners—shouldering their bags and carrying their bowls—were as numerous as the trees in a forest. Yet there was not one among them who did not claim to be seeking this Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*).
Although each was diligent in self-discipline and earnest in their application of mind, some were distracted by extraneous thoughts and strayed onto divergent paths;
others stole fine-sounding names to boast of themselves, or adorned their speech with empty words to deceive the world. Thus it was between master and disciple.
Deceiving one another like jellyfish that take shrimp for eyes, they hope to grasp the intent of the "Yellow-Faced Old Man’s" single transmission of the Dharma;
yet they remain far, far removed from it. In the past, when Chief Seat Yong and Ciming took their leave of Fenyang together, Yong had not yet fully mastered the subtlety of this seal of the Dharma.
He remained in the company of Ciming for twenty years, yet in the end—
He attained ultimate realization. One night, while they were gathered around a brazier late at night, Ciming struck the charcoal with a fire-tongs and called out, "Head Seat Yong!
Head Seat Yong! Yong retorted, "Wild fox spirit! Ciming then pointed at Yong and said, "What a clumsy fellow!"
Furthermore, it was by going in this way that Yong was finally able to receive this Great Dharma Seal into his hands. Observe Ciming:
having received this unsurpassed Dharma Seal from Fenyang, he was able to take error upon error and bring it forth for use;
indeed, he was able to treat the "sickness of no illness" of the Head Seat Yong. Nevertheless, even so, they could not avoid mutually obstructing one another. Pēngshān.
The Head Seat Yin came personally from the assembly of Master Zhe-weng. He profoundly understood the intent behind the Yellow-faced Old Man’s [the Buddha’s] single error of entrustment.

Having gathered with me in several places, he has already grasped the essentials of this unsurpassed Dharma-seal even before the time of the funeral pyre and the striking of the charcoal with a chopstick.
Soon, he shall take up this seal to stamp and break through the face-gates of all people. Truly...
This was transmitted by Master Zhuowei Yingshou, who represents the very root of "taking what is wrong and making it right.
He showed this to Head Seat Shaozhen (who previously resided at Nanchan in Quzhou):

"The Buddha-dharma is most subtle; its subtlety lies in the illumination of the mind. If the mind is thoroughly illuminated, the ten directions are completely penetrated. Since they are the ten directions..."
Thoroughly penetrating. It is just like this: when it is the third watch in the north, why is the sun not yet set in the west?
If you can see through this point, you will then see the Seven Patriarchs of India and the Two or Three Patriarchs of the Tang land;

you will see the old monks of the world where host and guest alternate, where staffs and shouts fly back and forth, where whisks are brandished and beds struck, where earth is moved and stones dragged, where staves are held aloft and fingers are raised, and where the ground is struck and heads are severed.
A snake. A single function, a single object; a single word, a half-phrase—all exist prior to the first excretion.
It only requires that you now, before your parents were born, realize your own original face. Then naturally all words will be shattered and every dharma destroyed.
When the wind stirs the dust or the grass moves, you will discern the subtle signs; in letting go and gathering back, there is no teaching left over. As for Muzhou...
Master Zhoushi was an eye among those beneath the great, cooling tree that is Linji; he likewise did not depart from this fundamental principle.
In the world today, those who possess such an eye are like the moon among the stars. Shaozhao the Head Seat was resolute in his pursuit of the Way;
with a mind full of earnest inquiry and words of profound hesitation, he had plumbed the depths and heights of all quarters and shared half of the seat on Vulture Peak. Already...
I have caught a glimpse of a single斑 (spot). Strive even harder from now on; do not begrudge these great eyes. Please try to point out one *jin* or half a *jin*.

Only then will the shade of the Great Tree provide cool relief for all under heaven. This will not only demonstrate that you surpass Muzhou and possess the spirit to "devour Linji alive," but it will also ensure that you do not fail the purpose of your lifelong travels as a pilgrim.
Baoshou, the Rector, requested words from me. As I recalled them, I remembered how Chan Master Yunfeng Yue visited Master Dayu Zhi;
he had no profound sayings or wondrous phrases to warn him, but simply said to him: "The Buddha-dharma..."
Fearing they would rot away, he took up various tasks—preparing charcoal, begging for food, and serving the assembly with joy—performing each duty without the slightest hint of reluctance.

Yet, he remained deeply resentful that Dayu had not explained the matter to him. While he was thus in a state of incessant frustration, he suddenly heard the sound of a wooden barrel箍 (gūn) bursting at the back of the hall.
In that instant, he attained sudden enlightenment and rushed to the abbot’s quarters. Upon seeing him, Dayu immediately said:

[The Master] said: "Venerable Vinaya Master, you may rejoice; the great matter is now concluded. Yet, when Yunfeng did not utter a single word, Dayu immediately declared that his 'great matter was concluded.
Dayu had initially spoken not a single word to warn him. Why, then, did Yunfeng attain awakening?
Generally speaking, this is the great furnace for smelting saints and ordinary beings, and the fierce tongs and hammers for forging Buddhas and patriarchs—a direct and authentic transmission."

Its longevity shall extend to future generations; its transmission shall be boundless; its bestowal shall be inexhaustible. One must be a man forged from iron in this very life, able to shoulder the burden with his entire being.
Only after hearing Yunfeng’s "one-time explosion of a wooden bucket" can one become a worthy successor of Bodhidharma.
Otherwise, my school will perish. Baocan, the *vina*, requested words as a means of admonition; thus, [I speak] for Yunfeng.
He showed him the circumstances regarding his meeting with Dayu. [The Master said:
"If you can further look back toward Yunfeng before you saw Dayu, and attain a single eye that is alive, then you will see that this monk’s failure is no small matter.
He then cast the words he had been shown into the fire, saying, "The great task of a true man is now complete."
To the Zen practitioner Shaolong (residing at Huiguo):
A student of the Way whose realization of the ground has not been liberated and whose intellectual understanding remains unforgetting falls into the poisonous sea of liberation.

When emotional consciousness has not yet been extinguished and the objects of consciousness are not empty, this is entirely a mass of deluded karmic consciousness. So long as this mass of deluded karmic consciousness is not shattered, it is the poison of liberation.
The ocean is never exhausted; it is precisely the very root of birth and death. If one wishes to forge the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it will take three lifetimes and sixty kalpas.

Yet, if one can simply let go from within this emptiness, overturning it to its very bottom, becoming uniquely liberated and without dependence, not violating even a single hair’s breadth—this is still not the place where a patch-robed monk moors his boat. Have you not seen what the Great Master Yunmen said? "Straight..."
To attain the exhaustion of the entire universe and the great earth, such that not even a hair’s breadth of fault or affliction remains—this is still a "turning phrase.
To not see a single color is but half the presentation. You must further know there is a time for the "total presentation.
But how is it that this is the time of the total presentation? If you can apply a living eye here, you will see Master Yunmen’s corpse lying across the entire world.
Bluntly: The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs must involve tearing one’s straw sandals to shreds before one can truly repay the vision cultivated throughout a lifetime of study.

The Way of daily practice shown to Master Zhi, the Guest Prefect (formerly the Supervisor of the Flower Medicine Garden in Hengzhou), does not reside within external things; it is the lineage not transmitted by the thousand sages, which is unconstrained.
This is the realm of profound mystery. Unless one is a person who stands firmly on solid ground, how could they be worthy of discussing this? Its subtlety lies in the turning point;
only when one perceives it thoroughly amidst all phenomena can the ancestral tradition that not even a thousand sages have transmitted manifest itself in every thought-moment.
The realm of profound mystery can be broken through and escaped from. The Way practiced daily and constantly accords with the tracks everywhere.
Once, when Huìtáng saw Huánglóng, the latter had a look of displeasure; Huìtáng therefore questioned him about it. Huánglóng said, "I have not yet found someone to serve as *jiānshōu* (overseer).
Huìtáng replied that Fùsì Gǎn could fill the post. Huánglóng said, "Gǎn is still violent; I fear he is too small [for the task]."
When people were discussing this, Huìtáng remarked, "Attendant Huà is somewhat upright and prudent. Huanglong said, "He is not as good as Zhuāngzhǔ Xiù, who possesses both capacity and loyalty.
Observe how Huanglong, in selecting a single supervisor (jiānsì), was so precise and discerning;
one can thus know that his samādhi for forging sages and melting commoners would never be bestowed upon anyone unworthy. Therefore, when practitioners of the Way reside [in a monastery], they must...
When the transformations of phenomena occur and one's violent nature suddenly erupts, it is rarely possible to achieve salvation.

If, however, you can conduct yourself with integrity and prudence in daily life and govern others with loyalty and clarity, then the essence that not even a thousand sages have transmitted—how could it be far away?
It is said that if one honors the Abbot (as seen in the *Zhuzu Pumen*),

traveling across rivers and seas and traversing mountains and streams to seek teachers and inquire after the Way for the purpose of Chan practice, once one has recognized the path of Caoxi, [one will proceed directly].
To realize that birth-and-death are not mutually involved—Master Yongjia, as soon as he opened his mouth, one could hear his local dialect.

If someone, before Yongjia had even opened his mouth, were able to set up a single eye of life, they would overturn the primordial oceans and rivers and trample the mountains and rivers of their own self;
there would be no Chan to investigate and no Way to seek, giving rise to the teacherless [awakening].
Wisdom—though it be spontaneous wisdom—the single path of Caoqi is right before one's eyes. The ancestral home of Nanmin does not dwell outside the mind.
Fully alive and fully dead, one is not constrained by birth and death; going and coming of one’s own accord, how could there be any obstruction to going and coming?
Thus, even before crossing the Feiyuan Ridge, one has already traveled through the monasteries of Jiang and Zhe, never departing from the Perfect [Enlightenment].

The Barrier of Awakening. Having already reached my hometown south of the sea, have you not seen how when Master Xuansha was traveling on pilgrimage to Feiyuan Ridge, he suddenly stepped on his own toe and blood flowed? Enduring the pain, he said, "This body is not mine; from where does the pain come?
Later, Xuefeng said to him, "Head Monk Bei, why do you not travel to visit all the teachers? Xuansha replied, "I have attained it."
"Polishing [the mirror] did not bring it to this eastern land; the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Dahui said: "These words were already late.
It should have been said at the very moment one touches the tip of one's toe and blood flows. Even so, one would still have avoided Xuefeng’s pointing and instructing.
If you ask whether Master Jing left the ridges to travel everywhere for study, I do not know if he ever touched his toe or not. If he had touched it..."
When he stepped on his toe and it bled, he did not know whether it occurred before he had left the mountain pass or after he had already left.
In this world, there was no Xuefeng to serve as a witness for you; nor do I, this mountain monk, possess the fixed eye that can verify the past and present for you.
However, from the moment Xuansha touched his toe and it bled, not only could Xuansha not bear the pain, but even now, [the suffering] remains entirely...
For those of the "Great Earth" rank, their endurance of pain is still not yet thorough. Do you not know whether the Librarian has ever awakened to this pain?
Even after thirty years, he will still not escape being scrutinized by others.
To Zen Practitioner Benran (Offering for the Assembly of Monks):
An ancient worthy said, "The Way is near, yet people seek it afar; the matter is easy, yet people seek it through difficulty.
Now, as for this Way and this matter—whether they are one or two—if you can discern them clearly, you will see that difficulty and ease, and the near and the far, are [not separate].
Near and far are both the wondrous functioning of my own self. Naturally, in every place and at every moment, this very mind is employed.
In every object and at every point, what further matter could there be? Even if right and wrong, gain and loss, reach their myriad transformations;

even if opposition and compliance, acceptance and rejection, present ten thousand variations in daily life—there is not one that is not a path for bringing people to life. You practitioners of the Way, you have reached such a field.

The Ground. How could it merely mean acting as master wherever one is, and taking up the essential principle whenever conditions arise? At all times and in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
whether facing adversity or favor, or moving vertically or horizontally—one does not stir so much as a hair’s breadth.

To grasp the world of Abhirati within the palm of one’s hand, and to take food from the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) realm above to satisfy thirty-two thousand beings—all these are the playful exercise of samādhi, winning the peripheral matters. So it is said:

By means of the Way. The Buddha-dharma is most subtle; its subtlety lies in the illumination of the mind. If the mind is thoroughly illuminated, the ten directions will be penetrated through and through.
At such a time, if one were to stand before the gate of a patch-robed monk, heaven and earth would be as vastly separated. The practitioner Benran was extremely resolute in his pursuit of the Way;

seeing that the three manors of the mountain gate had been submerged by water and the entire community lacked grain, he sacrificed more than a thousand strings of cash from his own resources to provide for them. I pray...
He converted all the donors and patrons; from then until the eighth month, he opened the gates of offerings to relieve the shortages of the permanent endowment.
Consequently, he came with paper in his sleeve seeking words [of instruction]. I praised the excellence of his resolve and asked him about the way of the patch-robed monks.

"What excellence do you possess? He replied, "Wait until my work of transformation is finished, and I shall explain it for you. I said, "A sharp and clever monk turns of his own accord without being pushed;
there will surely be someone along the way who hears the lute-string and appreciates the music."
To the Venerable Zhiming (formerly abbot of Ba’en in Yuanzhou):

How great is the mind! It is so vast that there is nothing it does not encompass; it is so subtle that there is nothing it does not penetrate. To add to it does not make it redundant; to diminish it does not cause it deficiency.
It operates silently of itself; it responds skillfully in stillness. It is swift without haste; it arrives without traveling.
Its square form cannot confine it, and its measurements cannot exhaust it. It is brilliantly manifest within the midst of daily life, yet there is no other reason why students fail to enjoy its use:
their emotional thoughts muddle it, and their profit-seeking desires cloud it. At its subtlest level, it becomes birth and abiding.
They are driven by the arising and ceasing of difference. At the coarse level, they are enslaved by earth, water, fire, and wind;

forgetting themselves to pursue external objects, they discard the true and grasp the false, ultimately ending in aimless wandering from which they do not return—this is the case for the entire world.

If one could but remove the obscurations of the mind and restore the foundation of its nature, clearly perceiving this mind within daily activities, then emotional conceptions, sensory desires, and the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—earth, [water, fire, and wind]... [would no longer hold sway].

Water, fire, and wind are all the wondrous functioning of my own self. By means of this, I adapt to conditions as they arise; what obstacle could there be then to birth and death, or coming and going?
Vinaya Master Kebin was once in the assembly of Xinghua when he was struck with a staff and driven out of the monastery.

This is what is meant by "refining fine gold through a hundred smeltings"; one must require the hammer of the fundamental division [of truth]. Were it not for Xinghua, he could not have carried out such an edict. Were it not for...

"Ke-bin was not enough to match him. Nevertheless, at the moment when Xing-hua issued his command, had there been a single person who clapped their hands and laughed heartily, one could have taken it for certain that Xing-hua and his son possessed a special excellence.
Since he let the matter pass at that time, tell me: how is the matter now? Please, Venerable Zhi-ming, come forward and provide a turning word.
Speech. To the Zen practitioner Jihyeong (who opened the reception hall):
Haejip is located at Hongjeupseon, which truly stands at a crossroads where the four directions meet and paths converge from all eight quarters. For anyone setting out on a journey to travel afar...
There are no noble persons who do not proceed by this path; yet our temple has long lacked permanent endowments, making it difficult to provide for these needs.

The Venerable Zhìyǐng, a preeminent talent among the mountain-dwellers, sighed and said: "I have traveled everywhere throughout the various regions, and wherever my feet have gone, I have been provided with the four requisites of monastic life."
"It is like returning to one's ancestral home. How could it be that I, a wanderer among clouds and waters coming and going from this region, have no place to rest?
For this reason, I have resolved to solicit offerings from the faithful throughout the ten directions to jointly accomplish this undertaking, and I beg you for your words. I said to him:

"Before the time of Baizhang, there was no responsibility for presiding over a monastery, nor was there any accumulation of even a foot of land. Those predecessors who had attained the Way hid themselves in deep mountains and remote valleys."

In the valleys, once the scent of meat and pungent flavors wafted upon the roads, scholars from the four quarters would pack their provisions and follow one another, hoping for a single word to liberate them from birth and death.

Therefore, at that time, there were those who attained liberation while sitting or passing away while standing; those who supported the lineage and established the teachings were found everywhere. Now it is not so.
Whenever people leave the monasteries and enter the sangha communities, traveling across rivers and seas or traversing mountains and rivers, wherever their footsteps reach—
Thus, they enjoy warmth and fullness. Yet, why is it that we hear nothing of even one person or half a person who has thoroughly penetrated this mind and magnified this Way?
Yong said: "Is it not so? Since antiquity has long passed, the faculties of people have become subtle and inferior.

Even those who wear grass for clothing and eat from trees, or dwell among mountains and sleep by waters, must inevitably suffer from the malady of collapse and an inability to revive the Way. This is what my ambition is directed toward."
This is indeed the fundamental intention of the Elder of Yellow Face regarding the City of Transformation and the Precious Abode.
I pray that you will write this down for me, so as to exhort all donors to collectively accomplish this task.

From this day forward, among those who come and go and find rest, how could there not be some who, bypassing the City of Transformation, ascend directly to the Precious Abode, possessing a distinct way of life? Furthermore, what need is there to worry about the mind?
It has not yet been fully realized; the Way is not so vast. What is spoken of as the era prior to Baizhang—how could it be distant?
I admire the breadth of his intent and have inscribed this to entrust to him. There will surely be those who understand your intention and realize this sublime connection.
To the Secretary Dechen:
The Secretary Dechen presented the "Song of the Playful Pearl" to this mountain monk. As I unrolled the scroll and observed it closely, I was suddenly dazzled by the pearl’s radiance;

east and west could not be distinguished, nor north and south. I did not know from where this pearl had come, yet the pearl— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

A thousand transformations and ten thousand shifts; moving freely in all directions. To play with this pearl is such a marvel! This mountain monk often laments that my brothers do not recognize this pearl;
they are turned by external objects and wander through the three realms. Occasionally, there are those who obtain this pearl;
they cherish it as a singular treasure and hold it dear as their own family jewel, refusing to let go. Within the light and shadows, it manifests of its own accord.
With supernormal powers, you have headed toward the ocean of liberation and manifested your own wondrous functions; yet there is no end to this.

This is precisely the root of birth and death, resembling a dung beetle clutching a ball of manure. It merely rolls it back and forth from clean ground, unaware of when to stop and oblivious to its own stench.
Suddenly, struck by someone, the ball of manure is smashed to pieces and the dung beetle is wiped out.

Originally, it was simply a single expanse of pure ground from the beginning. Brothers, now that you have obtained this pearl in your hands, it is precisely the right time to enter the great furnace and seek out a hammer of malice;
subject it to a thousand smeltings and ten thousand refinements until this pearl is consumed and its radiance is utterly forgotten.
The ocean of liberation has run dry; based on what precedes, it is simply the person of old. There are no such manifold supernatural powers, nor does one perform such wondrous functions.
All day long, one remains in a state of leisure, just like an ordinary person. Yet, when casually touched, fire spontaneously erupts from beneath the water.
Have you not seen how Master Nanquan addressed the monks, saying: "Thus he plays with the pearl and speaks of the pearl"?
"The light pervades everywhere. If there were a golden platter here, you would have obtained it. Suddenly, the golden platter is snatched away; where can one play with the pearl?
Where can one seek that light—whether it pervades or does not pervade? The monk bowed. Nanquan said, "Great difficulty, great difficulty!
The ancients would have cursed you, calling you a hunter, a fisherman, or a man who carries away excrement. The old man Nanquan is profoundly compassionate."
By means of parables and words, he causes people to recognize their own original pearl; yet they suddenly forget what they have understood.
This is merely intended to remove the golden platter, but it cannot, for this monk, shatter the pearl itself. For this reason, he is labeled a hunter or fisherman, and a carrier of filth.
A true man of great character, whose spirit swallows the Buddhas and patriarchs, would never learn the ways of hunting or fishing.
"Seize it! Those who work as dung-carriers will smash this pearl and make their living from its fragments; they will also be spared the labor of 'first gazing,' 'repeated gazing,' and 'third gazing.
It will flow forth from their very breast, covering heaven and earth, and only then will they not have betrayed the original intent of their lifelong practice.
Even so, tell me: ultimately, from where did this pearl come? Now, please speak."
The first turning phrase:
When staying as a guest at a layperson’s house, one who has attained realization reveals a message that is like heaven turning and earth revolving, like thunder rolling and wind blowing;
there is no place for you to approach, no place for you to settle. How could this wait for...?
To speak while reclining on a meditation bench and to write upon snowy paper—can this be considered the study of Zen? This mountain monk is no master;
I am merely an old monk prone to nodding off. Even the thousand sages would not know where my tracks lead.
Since you, Elder Jiding, have been with me for so long, even if you possess the eyes that recognize the fundamental principle the moment your feet cross the threshold, you will still know.
"Ichōzan has not yet been seen even in a dream. Now tell me, what excellence does Ichōzan possess? Try to examine this for yourself.
*The Recorded Sayings of Zen Master Chijetsu*, Volume Lower (End).
Epitaph for the Stupa.
In the *renzi* year of the Shaoxi era, I departed from the Gorges. During the summer at Ersheng Temple in Gong’an, Songyuan was propagating the teachings of Mian at Jianfu in Raozhou;

due to a severe drought, it was difficult to assemble a large congregation. It happened that the seat at Miaoguo on West Lake was vacant, and Songyuan proposed Cao Yuan, the former head seat of Yunju, to fill it.
Cao Yuan had also been a successor of Mian. I listened as he entered the gate.
Upon hearing his teachings, he attained realization and subsequently surrendered himself to him to reside there. Before long, he returned to serve in the administrative office.
In the summer of the Jia-yin year, he received an invitation from Cao Yuan to go to Mount Gui Peak and followed him there once more. He remained for three years before departing for Zhejiang.
When Songyuan moved from Huqiu to Lingyin, Dun’an took up residence at Huazang, and Kentang at Jingci; he visited and attended them all. While Songyuan was [at Lingyin]...
At Lingyin, the gate was solitary and steep. It was eight months before I was permitted to enter the hall. Anyone seeking to register for residency would invariably be scolded and denied access.
One day, he suddenly said, "I have opened the gates wide to admit them; from now on, they will miss their chance.
Only then did I realize that during my three years at Guifeng, Cao Yuan’s angry rebukes and playful laughter were all intended for this very purpose.
This was the expedient means of the man. From this point on, he no longer had doubts regarding the world’s elder masters; whether they reached him or not, none could deceive him.
Thereafter, he lived freely and expansively according to conditions. After Cao Yuan’s [Baizhang] peaceful passing, twenty years later, he was brought forth for the sake of others.
I dare not forget this single offering of incense. There have been brothers gathered in six different places; it cannot be said that they were nonexistent.
It is simply that those who employ the "method for blinding the eyes" are few. How bitter! Our school is being lost. This year I am eighty-two;

as the time [of my passing] approaches, I take up the pen despite my illness to directly record the origins of how I received the Dharma. I shall carve it upon the inner surface of my funerary niche to manifest ultimate sincerity. The tenth year of Chunyou.
Year [blank]. The year was Gengxu. On the sixth day of the third month, Chijue wrote this.
The Life Account of Chan Master Chijue of Mount Jing:
The master’s name was Daochong; he styled himself Chijue (Foolish Extinction). He was the son of Guo of the Gou clan from Changjiang in Wuxin. His mother, Lady Guo, once dreamed—
He was walking beneath a papaya tree when its fruit hung thick upon it. He plucked one and ate it; diviners declared that he would give birth to an extraordinary man.
Shortly thereafter, the boy was born with broad shoulders and short legs, possessing an endowment that surpassed others. When he grew up, he attempted the jinshi examination but met with failure.

He received the teachings of the Śākya clan at Miaoyin Monastery in Zizhou and received the tonsure under Master Xiuzheng. He traveled to Chengdu, where he studied the sūtras and śāstras at Dasheng Cisi Temple.
Before long, however, he grew weary of the conventional characteristics of worldly phenomena and developed a profound aspiration for the supramundane Dharma.
In the *Renzi* year of the Shaoxi era (1192), he left the Gorges region and traveled through the Jing and Chu areas. At that time, Songyuan Yue was propagating the teachings of Mian.
While traveling at Jianfu Monastery in Rāo, he went directly to his hut. It happened that there was a famine that year;

hearing that Cao Yuansheng was leading the assembly at Yunju and that Songyuan had been invited to take charge of Miaoguo on West Lake, the Master listened to his introductory words and attained realization.
He served as the attendant for incense while [Dongshan] visited the hall. In the summer of the Jiayin year, he followed him again when [Dongshan] moved to Guifeng.

He remained there for three years before departing for Zhejiang with a verse of farewell that included the lines: "There remains but this pair of hands, the mark of poverty; I intend to scratch the itchy spots throughout all quarters.

These words have been recited by the Jianghu community to this day. When Songyuan presided over Lingyin, his standards were lofty and steep, and he did not grant approval lightly. The Master... [resided there].
For eight months, he had not been permitted to enter the hall. He would often stammer, wishing to speak of his own accord, but was repeatedly rebuked and not allowed to approach.
One day, someone informed Songyuan of this. Songyuan said, "I have opened wide with my eight characters and accommodated him; it was simply that he himself missed the mark right before my face.
Upon hearing these words, the Master’s mouth and ears were both silenced; only then did he realize that while serving Cao Yuan...
During the time of Miaoguo and Guifeng, their laughter, jesting, scolding, and rebuking were all nothing other than skillful means (*upāya*).

From then on, he no longer harbored doubts regarding the tongues of the elder monks throughout the land. Subsequently, after the passing of Caoyuan, he traveled to the gates of various masters for more than twenty years.
When Jingtai Kenkang and Huazang Dun’an first beheld him, they recognized him as a vessel of the Dharma and knew his hidden potential.

As for the transmission of the Hermitage (An): it was destined to flourish again in later times. Subsequently, Qian’an Guang, Yi’ung Ru, Chidu Ying, Yan-shi Kai, and Zhe’ung Yan all shared half his seat, being commissioned to propagate his teachings.
In the Jiajia Jimao year, he departed from Mount Jing to accept the invitation of Guangxiao Monastery in Jiaxing;
with a single incense stick, he served as the source of Cao Yuan and offered his final memorial service. In the Baoping Yiyou year...

He received an official decree and was transferred to Mount Jiangshan. At Mount Jiangshan, the fields were extensive; situated between mountains and water, the region suffered from unpredictable droughts and floods.

Consequently, the annual rent was insufficient to support the community. The Master endured austerity in his food and lived simply, finding peace in solitude. For fourteen years, he remained steadfast from beginning to end as if it were a single day.
At that time, Chen Gong, whose courtesy name was Yizhai, was serving as the Commander-in-Chief at Jinling. He had long respected the Master’s solitary integrity of conduct.
Gao presented this to the Governor of Min, Cao Dongquan. As the seat at Gushan was vacant, Cao immediately appointed the Master to preside over it.
Before long, he was transferred to Xuefeng. He entered the monastery in the Wuxu year of the Jiashih era; barely half a year had passed when—
The gist is as follows: He resided at the famous mountain Taibai. At that time, the Abbot of Yungwang Monastery had been unable to find a successor.

Because the Master arrived, he was strongly urged to accept the position, and thus he concurrently presided over both institutions. The Master traveled back and forth between the two mountains, and scholars from all quarters flocked to him like people returning to a bustling market.
His reputation reached the capital. In the year Jiachen of the Chunyou era...

By imperial decree, he was transferred to Lingyin Monastery to preach the Dharma at the foot of Feilai Peak. There, he recalled his former travels with Mian and Songyuan and contemplated how to revitalize the ancestral tradition;
yet, demonic obstacles arose beyond his expectations, such that they could not be resolved through mere words.
He suddenly felt a renewed resolve to spend the remainder of his life on his home mountain and struck the drum to depart in haste, despite the efforts of Zhao Jiezhai, the Prefect of Jingzhao.

The Duke sent a letter earnestly urging him to return, and an official decree from the Hall (Tangti) appointed him to Tiger Hill (Huiqiu). Master Sheng was also invited by Zhao Gong of Xuzhai from Mount Jiangshan;
yet none could turn his mind. In the spring of Wushen, the assembly at Yuyang Temple dispersed, and the great elders were as sparse as morning stars.
Only the Master remained as a venerable patriarch of the monastic community (*conglin*), and the multitude petitioned the court for him, waiting day and night for the Master’s arrival.

He departed, yet firmly declined the invitation until it was finally desisted. The following year, the year of Jiyou (1269), he visited Chancellor Hongyi You Gong and Minister Cangzhou Cheng Gong at their private residences by the Tiaoxi River.
On his return journey, Zhao Gong of Jiezhai in Jingzhao sent a messenger on horseback with a letter.
While on the road, he lingered at the provincial seat for over two weeks. [The governor] wished to entice him to be the founding patriarch of Fahua Monastery, entreating him earnestly several times;
however, he could not grant the request.
Subsequently, an imperial decree arrived appointing him to reside at Jingshan. The Master said, "I have already given my word, and it would certainly be improper to go back on it."
How could he have been required to yield his position by imperial decree? In the ninth month, he arrived at Fahua; over a month later, he ascended Shuangjing.

He was truly following in the footsteps of Wuzhun Fayan; men and spirits converged in reverence, and the sound of joyful acclaim was like thunder. Suddenly, he contracted an illness in the region between his heart and diaphragm.

His food and drink diminished day by day. From winter through spring, although his physical form grew emaciated, he ascended the hall to lead the assembly with a clarity and vigor as if nothing were amiss.
On the sixth day of the third month, he suddenly wrote a record for his funerary niche, recounting the origins of his transmission of the Dharma.
He dispatched some ten letters and, moreover, dictated a dharma discourse to be sent to the stupa of Wuzhun, saying: "The anniversary of Wuzhun’s passing falls on the eighteenth. I..."
"On the fifteenth day, I shall depart immediately; I cannot perform the offering of split incense. The attendant monk was startled by these words and requested the Master's final verse.
The Master smiled and said, "The final word is not something to be deliberated upon; it requires only that a person directly take it up."
He immediately took up his brush and wrote a message for the assembly before ascending the hall, saying: "When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, he addressed the assembly, saying:
'You should carefully observe my purple-golden body; gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied, lest you have cause for regret later.
Today it exists, but tomorrow it will be gone. [The Master] added: "Throughout his life, the World-Honored One exhausted every skill and artifice; yet at the moment of death, he sought..."
To live, he could not live; to die, he could not die. I, this mountain monk, am otherwise: when I wish to walk, I walk; when I wish to go, I go. Eight-armed Nala cannot block me;
I simply set aside physicians and cast away medicines. Indeed, at the hour of midnight on the fourteenth day, he rose from his seat and passed away after remaining so for a short while.
Three days later, his body was cremated, and the *śarīra* relics were brilliant, shimmering in five colors. His younger brother...
His disciple followed his final instructions and enshrined his sacred remains, returning them for burial at Yushan Hermitage in Jinling on the nineteenth day of the fifth month of the Gengxu year.

His students, unable to bear their grief, divided half of the remains to construct a stupa at Yuzhi Hermitage in Changpu Field on Mount Jing, which took place on the twenty-fourth day of that same month.
He was eighty-two years of age and had been a monk for sixty-one years. Thus ends the account of the Master.

He was pure and sincere without guile, consistent in both outward appearance and inner character. He treated others with forgiveness while maintaining strict discipline over himself; he responded to the world with adaptability yet led his assembly with solemnity.

Having lived on the mountain for thirty years, wherever he went, he took it as his personal responsibility to revitalize the spirit of the school, and he regarded it as his own concern that the Dharma had not yet found its successor.
In his daily life, he was simple, serene, and silent, appearing as if unable to speak; yet when deliberating matters, he was incisive and decisive.

In his quarters, he would examine and test his disciples; a single touch of his spiritual pivot was like the rushing of thunder and the flashing of lightning, or the surging of the sea and the overturning of rivers, leaving all utterly bewildered and unable to find a point of entry.
He vowed never to lightly grant his favor through word or expression to others, lest he further mislead those who came to study under him.

In his later years, he had no other interests and devoted much attention to the art of calligraphy; regarding small-character script (*xiaokai*), he attained mastery (*samādhi*). His work was often upright, dignified, and solemn.
People of both monastic and lay status venerated him; there was not a single day that he did not receive requests for Dharma discourses, verses, or eulogies.

Despite the bitter cold or intense heat, he never grew weary of taking up his brush to paint. Many scholar-officials delighted in following him as a companion, and he was especially esteemed by renowned dukes and high ministers.
Consequently, his fame spread abroad until it reached overseas lands, where some came to inquire after him, braving the surging waves and bringing with them formal letters of introduction.

As for the Dharma, its moral virtue is such that it can subdue others; it has reached this very point. It was during the time of Emperor Yuzong of Tiantong that he received an imperial decree to open the hall at Lingyin.
As he packed his bags and prepared to depart with his precepts and conduct, a neighbor-peak monk who harbored malice toward him raised his voice, intending to incite trouble.

A great multitude of unruly elements caused obstructions along the way. When those on the left and right heard of this, they raised the matter to inform the Master, saying, "In our daily life, we have treated others with sincerity;
how could we possibly add anything further to you? Yet he remained entirely unmoved. They, too, ultimately desisted, having found no means to influence him.
Shuangjing, Lingquan, Taibai, and Xuefeng are the preeminent monasteries within the realm. In recent years, however—

Those who harbor thoughts of haste and ambition rely on secret alliances and boast of their cleverness; they ascend the steps through intellectual artifice, believing their strength can even commune with the divine.
Master [Dao’an] was not like this. Clad in coarse hemp and plain cloth, he remained so until the end of his life, unmoved by power or profit.

Therefore, his advancement did not depend on intermediaries, and his withdrawal from office was always characterized by a tranquil mind. He was truly a pillar of the Dharma-gate and a model for later students.
This is the standard. Zhongfu Hill is sixty *li* from Dongyang, and Yushan lies precisely between them.

As he traveled upward from Runzhou, his monk’s staff passed through the area, yet he never paused there. When he set down his pack, the Master cleared away the brush to build a hut and chiseled stones to open a path.

All that was in his bag and bowl was insufficient to cover the expenses for the construction work. The Master of Jinghu... *(Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available fragment.)*
Upon hearing of this, Lord Anmeng and Lord Qiuhuo Jia provided assistance. Lord Jiezhai Zhao, the Prefect of the Capital, subsequently donated gold and grain to aid in its completion.
Thereupon, adjacent to the hermitage, the site for interring the remains was determined; it is surrounded by encircling peaks with the "Dragon" and "Tiger" hills facing one another.
It fully captures the elegance of all the mountains of Jinling, where jasper peaks and jasper fungi abound.

The names [of the master and his disciple] were perfectly suited to one another; how could this have been by mere chance? Therefore, when he passed away, his burial was conducted according to his own wishes.
One month after the interment, his dharma-heir, Fajian, sent the teacher’s final letter and entrusted his life story to me, Youju, requesting that I compose a formal biography.
I, however, am currently secluding myself in the countryside and have long been afflicted by illness, leaving me with no leisure for such a task. Two years passed...
Tu Liao-yuan, holding the preface and introduction to the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) composed by the Minister You Gong, earnestly renewed his previous request for instruction.
He lamented that in the spring of the Bingshen year, he had first met the Master at the foot of Dulonggang; upon their first encounter, they felt as though they were old friends.
Now, looking back, seventeen years have passed. Feeling that his sense of duty could not allow him to decline, he has thus compiled the accounts from the records gathered by the Master’s disciples.
Truly, I have interspersed this with what I have heard, arranging the sequence from beginning to end and receiving the direct transmission of its source.

I thus entrust this to those great calligraphers of our time to request a commemorative inscription, so that it may serve as an imperishable record for the monastic community. I respectfully submit this report.
On the first day of the sixth month in the twelfth year of Chunyou, Zhao Ruju— holding the rank of Chao-san-lang, newly appointed Acting Governor of Nanxiong Prefecture and its Military Command,
concurrently overseeing agricultural affairs within the jurisdiction, and wearing the purple robe— submitted this memorial.

The abbot of Yuzhi Hermitage at Mount Jing, the venerable Master Yuan, brought the *Recorded Sayings* of the Elder Chijue to request that I compose a biographical sketch for him. He remained for over a month, his discourse resonant and clear, his voice deep and flowing;
he was truly a dragon or an elephant among the assembly. Upon our parting, I wrote two verses in quatrain to present to him as a gift.
On the Road. Old Man Ruan (Ruoju): The heat enters my single-layered linen robes, and the rain weighs down the dust.
Knocking at the gate, I am still pleased by the frequent arrival of guests. At leisure, I shall explain for you the meaning of the Westward Transmission;
The cypress in the courtyard is lush and green—truly pleasing to the spirit.
The truth of the secret, single-lineage transmission: with each raising [of the staff], there is something ever new. This is the teacher’s earnest final word;
one who can directly take it up is truly required.

Written on the first day of the sixth month in the Renzi year of Chunyou (1292) at the Jingshou Hall by Xu Minzi, a rustic recluse from Xiuyue. These humble offerings are presented along with a verse. Respectfully submitted.
Chan Master Anzhu:

Chijue had a hut he was unwilling to occupy; instead, he played with old clouds as he departed for Mount Yunju. When earth, water, fire, and wind were about to disintegrate, he personally wrote a gift of yellow hemp cloth for me.
Having unsealed the package and finished reading it, I was choked with silence; having realized the power of the dragon’s whiskers, I could do nothing more.
Dispelling the summer heat—how could one know that his jade bones were fundamentally cool? As for the calligraphy, he treasures it and does not take it to be spread abroad.

Old Yuan has suddenly trodden upon a path deep in the shadows; the Way lies in the distance, beyond the mountain peaks. His great volumes already carry idle entanglements; how can he bear to send yet more idle furniture?
Opening one's eyes to look at them, one laughs heartily: there is still this very thing, what can be done about it? It comes.
Not going forth is not a worldly dharma; I offer this meager tribute of my sincere devotion, though I am ashamed it is not much.
Two-cornered tea, ten bags of flour, and fifty thousand flying coins for the precious vase—I reverently offer this single incense stick as a pure memorial offering for the Chan Master.
Now I ask: will the former master come or not? At the summit of Mount Yu’s hermitage, the azure clouds part. Furthermore, I trouble the great assembly to strike the perfect circle.
He plucked the ashes of the blue lotus from within the fire.
In serving his master, it was not difficult for him to live; it was difficult for him to die.

When the Master Yuanliao sent word that the Venerable Chijue had passed away, he disregarded his own person and, amidst great hardship and distress, took charge of this momentous matter, compiling and circulating [the master’s teachings].
To achieve what is difficult without regarding it as difficult—
is this not truly admirable? Xiuyue and Lanyou.
All were my elder friends beyond the secular world. I presented him with a *geya* (verse) to encourage him to persevere through his hardships;
it was largely based on what I had learned from my elder. It was as if Wugou were engaging in a "tangled vine" debate with Miaoxi.

Later, Lao’er wrote an epitaph for his stupa to contain his remains and instructed Yuan to have it carved between the two huts. Whether it be "Jade Mountain" or "Jade Mushrooms," would not even Jiangjing know of it?
This old man does not die. All the elder monks of the world likewise know that this old man does not die.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of Baoyu, the bhikṣu Kūshan (Gentuan) respectfully appends these words.
The true lineage of Dongshan has not a trace of breath remaining. Even those who have "lost it" at the simultaneous moment of the chick pecking and the hen tapping have not yet dreamed of this.

Great Chan Master Chijue of Jingshan—whether speaking or not speaking, whether concise or expansive—has cast before everyone that which even Gautama could not open his mouth upon for seven places. Yet, alas, throughout the entire world, no one can grasp it by touch.
Searching for it, one finds nothing. This is simply because the teacher himself does not know where it lands. Reaching this point, he snaps his fingers once and sweeps his sleeves away, departing;
even if one tries to apply [the teaching], it is of no use. But tell me, where exactly does the error lie?

"Two rows of tears upon the coral pillow—half are thoughts of you, half are resentments toward you. Written on the evening of the full moon in the fifth month of the Xinhai year of the Chunyou era, respectfully by Yan Ru-xun.
Record. In the Wuxu year of the Jiaxi era, I was serving as the acting governor of Siming. In the following Jihai year, the elder Chizong Chong came to Tiantong;

on one occasion he visited my provincial residence, where we conversed cordially throughout the day, our hearts in perfect accord. In the Jiachen year, by imperial decree, I was transferred to Lingyin, where the school of our lineage flourished greatly.
Yang [Shanlin] one day shook out his robes and departed; he was establishing a central pillar for the Dharma realm and made no plans to remain beneath the mulberry trees.
In the year Yisi, he visited me in Jinling, where I invited him to stay at Mount Jiangshan. The Master said, "As soon as this old monk spreads his sitting cloth..."

Disciples from the four quarters gathered like clouds. This mountain’s resources were meager; for fourteen years I resided there, going out to beg for alms to provide the morning gruel and evening rice.
Now that I am old, I can no longer do so. I have vacated my seat and entrusted it to Baoning to manage concurrently, specifically to serve the Master.
In the year Dingwei, I was summoned back, and the Master also entered Zhejiang, where he received an imperial decree to preside over the abbotship of Mount Jing. Furthermore—

He passed beyond me, coming and going for twelve years as if we had first met. In the third month of the Gengxu year, he left me a letter and a verse, and presented a bronze incense burner and an ancient mirror as parting gifts.
I sighed with sorrow, lamenting that such a person would no longer be among us, and that the Buddha-dharma was becoming obscure.
I once asked the Master about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma; the Master said, "Whatever you do during the day—all of it is it."
Mencius said, "The gentleman desires that he attain [the Way] for himself. When one attains it for oneself, one dwells in it securely and draws from it deeply;
whether turning left or right, one encounters its source. But tell me, in this "attaining for oneself," what is it that is attained? To realize it here and now is itself the Buddha-dharma.
On the *Xinhai* year, his disciple Liaoyuan brought forth the Master’s *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) and showed it to me, saying, "The *Yulu* consists of ten fascicles; I have now taken these."
This single fascicle circulating in the world is, for the most part, a compilation by the Master’s own hand. I have therefore recorded this at the end of the scroll and returned it [to him].
On the mid-month day of the summer retreat, the rustic guest from Yunquan, Zhao Yifu.
Supplementary Verses in Praise of the Buddha’s Attainment of Enlightenment
Before the Mountain of Perfect Enlightenment, the eyes were lost; both ordinary and sage beings are born blind. To this day, every night the bright star appears;
who is willing to walk where it walks?
At the mountain of the Buddha’s nirvana, the flowers are like brocade and the waters like indigo; everything the eye touches is radiant as the spring reaches its full bloom.
If one says that he passed into extinction beneath the twin śāla trees, one has clearly missed the mark regarding the old Gautama.
The second patriarch’s single arm fell cold with the frosty blade; snowflakes parted as they fell, reaching his waist. Seeking the mind, he found nothing;
having finally attained peace of mind, he traveled to the source only to encounter a broken bridge.
The Third Patriarch thoroughly understood that the nature of sin is originally non-existent; after his life was severed, how could he ever have been restored?
It was originally but a chronic illness from before, which caused him to have his arm cut off and be forcibly plastered over with falsehoods.
The entire body is but illness, bones adhering to skin; throughout the world, no one recognizes him.
Even if one were to completely repent for the roots of all transgressions, one would still lose both eyebrows as before.
The Fourth Patriarch swept away the pit of former liberation; on the road of the Double Stream, no one passes. To his dying day, he made no handover of robe or bowl;
he pressed the man who planted the pine tree until death and rebirth.
At the summit of Pòtóu Peak, he closed the Chan gate; thrice declining the imperial summons, he did not descend the mountain. In the end, he possessed not the slightest breath of life;
what face could he have had to behold the Dragon’s countenance?
The Fifth Patriarch personally planted ten thousand pines; now that he has grown old, he can no longer strive to keep pace. How pitiable is Zhou’s daughter by the stream;
she too has been seduced and led astray by him.
The Sixth Patriarch gathered seven hundred eminent monks in a single assembly for Chan; his eyes looked across the four seas, his nose reached beyond the heavens.
Had Huangmei been without partiality or bias, how could there have been a robe or bowl passed down to you?

The water-lily flower has been crushed to pieces—already a muddled confusion. The matter of transmitting the robe at midnight grew ever more complex. From this point on, the profound path of Caoxi was severed;
without wind, the night ripples into waves that strike the heavens.
In discussing destiny, there is the "True Person of No Rank," stark and bare; who knows as he enters and exits through the gateway of the face? The Great Void shares its very same lifespan with him;
on this day of Gengshen, I rely on you, sir, to examine it closely.

The mother who returned home to visit her kin has revealed her true face; she is neither distant nor intimate, neither estranged nor close. Try asking the traveler returning home at the gate along the road:
"Who is the one leaning against the door?"
Water-lamps stretch across ten thousand li of misty waves into the pure autumn; silver lamps shine steadfastly as they float upon the central current.
Since that first point of radiance appeared, they have followed the surges and trailed the ripples, refusing to cease.
This chart of the lineages has been established to define the various schools; thread upon thread they interlace like a string of pearls. One wonders:
before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had yet appeared, was there not already much news?
Having cast off the body atop the mountain of the five aggregates with a broom of reeds, the thatched hut thereby transcends all comparison. Time and again, one employs it as it comes to hand;
let the great earth be taught to be free from even a speck of dust.
In making this "face-bucket," no effort was expended; in its use, there is no leakage whatsoever. Even though one’s nostrils may reach the heavens, one cannot avoid bowing the head to meet it.
(Recorded in the summer of the Jichou year of the Bao Yong era [1709], revised and transcribed within the Longxing Chamber).
From the *Suīyǐn Mànlù*, fascicle five, compiled by Chén Suīyǐn of Línchuān during the Sòng dynasty: "Empress Yán received a special imperial edict."
[The Master] seized the vegetable garden of Lingyin Monastery to build Gongde Monastery. When he was about to retire, the incumbent Chong Chijue addressed the assembly, saying:
"If you wish to go but do not go, you are hindered by going; if you wish to stay but do not stay, you are hindered by staying.
To be entirely unhindered—ten islands and three archipelagos are the realm of cranes; the four seas and five lakes are the world of dragons. Suoyin commented: "Does Changchang still have [this]?"
"Person. [The Master] looked at the Abbot, and there was none.
